source: Start with the core idea of a while loop: it keeps running “while” a loop expression is true, and it re-checks that expression before each new iteration. Anchor with the reading’s phrasing: “A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true.” Emphasize the two moving parts: (1) loop expression, (2) loop body.
target: Warm-up + definition of a while loop: repeat the loop body while a loop expression stays True, and re-check the loop expression before each new iteration. Put the anchor quote on the board: “A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true”. Ask students to predict what happens for a loop that stops (condition becomes False) versus one that never stops (condition never becomes False).

source: Worked example re-teach (from the reading): “n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1 prints 3, 2, 1 and then stops when n reaches 0.” Walk the trace step-by-step: show each time you evaluate the loop condition, then execute the body, then update n, then re-check the condition again. Anchor with: “At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again.”
target: Worked example walkthrough (from the reading): n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1 prints 3, 2, 1 and then stops when n reaches 0. Step through iteration-by-iteration: (1) n=3, condition n>0 is True → print 3 → update n=n-1 → n becomes 2; (2) check again → print 2 → update to 1; (3) check again → print 1 → update to 0; (4) check again: n>0 is False → loop terminates. Re-emphasize the quote: “At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again”.

source: A while loop terminates only if something the condition depends on changes during the loop. For a counter loop, update the counter inside the body (e.g., n = n - 1 or += 1) so the condition eventually becomes false. Also, the loop condition is checked only at the top of each iteration, after the current pass runs.
target: A while loop must eventually make its condition false, so update the variables the condition depends on inside the body. For a counter loop, include something like n = n - 1 (or += 1) so termination happens; otherwise the loop can become infinite. Also, the condition is checked only at the top of each iteration, after the rest of the current body runs.

source: Termination depends on making progress toward ending the loop expression. source: Scope is where a variable can be accessed; variables created inside a function have local scope and only exist within that call. Variables created outside any function have global scope and can be accessed anywhere. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.
target: Scope mini-lesson: explain variables as “the part of the program where the variable can be accessed.” Use the kernel phrasing: “A variable's scope is the part of a program where the variable can be accessed,” then contrast local vs global using the kernel facts: inside a function is local (only exists within that call), outside is global (accessible anywhere).

source: Worked example walkthrough again (functions & scope): start from this helper idea—def square(n): return n * n. Then ask: (1) Does defining it run the body? (No.) (2) What does square(5) produce? (25.) (3) If a variable inside the function (say result) is created only within the call, can code outside read it directly? (No—local scope. To use a value outside, return it and capture the returned value.)
target: Worked example: the reading’s square function. Start from: def square(n): return n * n. Point out what def does (store the function) vs what square(5) does (runs the body). Show the value flow: square(5) runs the body and returns 25. Then connect to scope: any variable created inside square would be local to that call; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture it.

source: Launch recursion: define it using the reading’s framing—“Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem”—and connect it to the mechanics: a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input, continuing until it’s small enough to solve directly (base case). Emphasize the termination requirement: without a base case that stops self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.
target: Warm-up and framing: recursion as problem-solving by reducing to a simpler version of the same problem. Read aloud the core idea: “Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem.” Emphasize that a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and must eventually reach a base case so it terminates. Quick check: why recursion without a stop condition “without it the calls would never stop” (call stack overflow).

source: Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. Without that stop, the self-calls continue until the call stack overflows. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.
target: Every recursive function needs a base case: a simplest input you can solve directly without making another self-call. Without that stopping condition, the self-calls never end and you eventually overflow the call stack. Each call must also move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g., n → n-1).

source: A class is the blueprint for creating objects. Individual objects created from a class are called instances, and each instance carries its own copy of the attributes while the methods are shared by every instance.

Emphasize: each object built from a class is an instance, and per-object data lives on the instance while methods defined by the class are shared across instances.

source: Debugging vs. testing in Python: define a test as an input/output check—if the output differs from the expected result for a specific case, that test fails and indicates a bug. Contrast syntax errors (program can’t run) with runtime errors (program starts, then exceptions like ZeroDivisionError happen). Explain how print statements (or a debugger) help reveal intermediate values and execution order, then use traceback information to pinpoint the line(s) where the runtime error occurred.
target: Debugging vs. testing. Define a test as an input/output check: if the program’s output differs from the expected result for a specific case, the test fails and indicates a bug. Contrast syntax errors (prevent running) with runtime errors (occur after the program starts, e.g., ZeroDivisionError). Introduce the practical workflow: (1) run a few tests, (2) add print statements to reveal intermediate values and execution order, (3) use the exception type + traceback to locate where behavior diverges.

source: Begin algorithms: an algorithm is a finite, well-defined set of steps that produces an output from an input and terminates. Translate a flowchart-style description into Python control structures (if/elif/else, for/while). Introduce correctness reasoning with invariants / loop conditions: loop conditions and invariants help ensure both correctness and termination. Then introduce time complexity by counting how the number of basic operations grows with input size n, often summarized with Big-O.
target: From intended algorithm to implementable code. An algorithm is a finite, well-defined set of steps that produces output from input and terminates. Connect reasoning to correctness/termination: loop conditions and invariants help ensure termination. source: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().
target: Local variables only exist during the call that created them, so to use a computed result outside the function you must return it and have the caller capture the return value. Separately, defining a function only stores it (it runs when called by name like greet()), and in loops the condition is checked only at the top of each iteration, after the rest of the current pass runs.

source: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Writing def greet(): does not run the function body immediately.
target: Defining a function only stores it, and the function body runs later when you call it by name (such as greet()). Simply writing def doesn’t execute the code inside the function.

source: Because a while loop tests its condition only at the top of each iteration, the body must change something the condition depends on. For a counter loop, use n = n - 1 or += 1 inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.
target: A while loop must update something the condition depends on; for a counter, you typically do n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. source: Every recursion needs a base case: a simplest input solved directly without another call, so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.
target: Recursion needs a base case—an input that can be solved directly without another recursive call—so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. Each recursive call must move toward that base case by shrinking the problem (e.g., n - 1); otherwise the base case is never reached.

source: With recursion, you must include a base case; without one, self-calls never stop and the call stack overflows. It also isn’t enough to “make the input smaller”—each call (e.g., `n - 1`) has to move toward the base case, or the base case is never reached. Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.
target: Recursion needs a place to stop: add a base case where the simplest input is solved directly without another call, so self-calls eventually end. Also ensure each recursive call moves toward it by shrinking the problem (e.g., n - 1), or the base case will never be reached.

source: Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms counts as a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included. Geometry is one model, not the definition, so arrows are only one example of vectors. A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.
target: For students coming in cold, re-state the core idea plainly: vectors are not defined by geometry. Then check the two requirements that separate a subset from a vector space: it must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

source: Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries. The leading positions in echelon form identify the pivot columns.
target: Close by naming pivots and reading echelon form: a pivot is the first nonzero entry of a row in echelon form, and pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries. source: A linear system cannot stop at two solutions. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.

source: Reteach pivot/row-operation reasoning with a targeted walkthrough of what students often mix up: show that elementary row operations do not change the solution set (swap, scale by nonzero, add multiple). target: For students arriving cold: row reduction uses elementary row operations to simplify a system without changing its solution set. source: Matrix multiplication is built from row-by-column dot products, not entrywise products. The entrywise rule belongs to a different operation, so it does not give AB; the product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products.
target: Matrix multiplication is not entrywise. The correct rule is: "The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation." That row-by-column structure determines each (i, j) entry.

source: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so order matters and AB can differ from BA. Being invertible does not make the products commute; order matters in matrix products, and AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.
target: Do not import the commutative law from ordinary numbers. "Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix." In general, reversing the order changes the result.

source: No, the determinant is multiplicative for products: det(AB)=det(A)det(B), but det(A+B) usually differs from det(A)+det(B).
target: No—this mixes up the product rule with a nonexistent sum rule. The determinant is multiplicative, not additive: det(AB)=det(A)det(B), but det(A+B) usually differs from det(A)+det(B).

source: Large entries do not prevent determinant 0; the determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size. That is why a matrix of large numbers can still collapse area or volume to zero.
target: Think geometric, not entry-by-entry: the determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size; a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero.

source: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so order matters and AB can differ from BA. Being invertible does not make the products commute; order matters in matrix products, and AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.
target: Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix. That is why matrix algebra is not like ordinary number multiplication.

source: Subspaces: build the checklist. A subspace is a subset that contains the zero vector AND is closed under addition AND scalar multiplication. Then connect the idea of span: linear combinations of given vectors always form a subspace, and the span is the smallest subspace containing them.
target: Use the reading's core examples: decide whether a subset is a vector space or a subspace by checking zero, closure under addition, and closure under scalar multiplication. Then connect span to subspace: the span of a set is all linear combinations, so it is always a subspace and is the smallest subspace containing those vectors. Tie this to column space and null space as concrete subspaces students will meet in matrix problems.

source: This is the inconsistency case: "A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet." So there is no solution to the original system.
target: Those two equations describe parallel lines with no intersection, so there is no solution. The corrective is: "A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet."

source: This is the inconsistency case: "A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet." So there is no solution to the original system.

source: Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. So a finite count larger than one does not happen for linear systems.
target: Once you have two distinct real solutions, every point on the line through them also solves the system, so there are infinitely many solutions. source: Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method. The point is not that the entries look nicer; it is that the solution set stays the same.
target: Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method. So the row replacement does not change which x-values solve the original system.

source: Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries. A large entry is not automatically a pivot; the row-reduction structure decides that.

source: Matrix multiplication is built from row-by-column dot products, not entrywise products. The entrywise rule belongs to a different operation, so it does not give AB; the product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products.
target: The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation. So you do not multiply corresponding entries the way you do for addition.

source: Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling. The origin condition is not optional.
target: A line through the origin works because it contains the zero vector and is closed under scaling. To rule out the others, use the corrective directly: "Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling."

source: Matrix-of-transformation idea (computation rules): when we multiply matrices, the (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Emphasize operations: addition and scalar multiplication are entrywise, but the matrix product AB is not entrywise multiplication. Also emphasize order: in general AB ≠ BA, and a product may not even be defined.
target: Move to matrix algebra: addition and scalar multiplication act entrywise, but matrix product is different. source:
A linear system over the real numbers has exactly two distinct solutions. What must be true?
The system is inconsistent

The system has infinitely many solutions
The system must have no free variables

source: Two equal rows force a zero determinant, so the matrix is nonzero yet not invertible. A square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse.
target: A square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse. So “nonzero” is not enough; invertibility depends on the determinant/pivots, not just on having some nonzero entry.

source: For an n-by-n matrix A, it is diagonalizable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Also, if you find eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues, you may treat them as automatically linearly independent when counting toward that n.
target: Diagonalizability is tied to having a full eigenvector basis: an n-by-n matrix is diagonalizable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Distinct eigenvalues help because their eigenvectors are automatically linearly independent, but you still need enough of them.

source: A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero. That is the key distinction: zero eigenvalue does not force every entry of A to vanish.
target: A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero. So the safe conclusion is singularity, not that every entry of A is zero.

source: Warm-up: what is a “value” vs a “variable”? Explain that every Python value has a data type (int, float, str, bool). source: Use explicit conversion: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text. The worked example states: “‘Age: ' + str(19) builds 'Age: 19', while 'Age: ' + 19 raises a TypeError because a str and an int cannot be added.”

source: The / operator performs true division and always returns a float, while // performs floor division and discards the remainder to give a whole-number quotient.

source: The correct fix is to convert the number to text first, or use formatting. Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. Wrapping a number in int() does not make it text.

source: Conditionals mechanics: if runs only when the condition is true; else runs only when the if condition is false. Emphasize the “one and only one branch is taken” idea, and reinforce what a condition actually is (an expression that evaluates to True/False).
target: Start with the decision idea: an if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when false. Then add else: the else clause runs when the if condition is false. Emphasize “one and only one of the branches is taken” for if-else.

This matches the provided worked example: if temp > 100: print('boiling') else: print('not boiling') — the else branch runs only when temp > 100 is false. In an if-else, one and only one branch is taken.

source: Start with the core idea of a while loop: it keeps running “while” a loop expression is true, and it re-checks that expression before each new iteration. Anchor with the reading’s phrasing: “A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true.” Emphasize the two moving parts: (1) loop expression, (2) loop body.
target: Start with the core definition: a while loop runs its body while a loop expression stays true, and the condition is re-checked before each new iteration. Emphasize the termination idea: if the loop condition never becomes false, the program runs forever (infinite loop), so the body must make progress toward ending the condition. Anchor with: “A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true.”

source: While loops mechanics + the two biggest failure modes: (a) forgetting to update the variable the condition depends on leads to an infinite loop; (b) assuming the condition is re-checked mid-body right when you change a variable. Anchor the timing: the loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before it’s checked again.
target: Reteach the two failure modes using the exact corrective language: (1) Updating the condition variable inside the body so the loop condition eventually becomes false: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” (2) When the condition is checked again: “The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.”

source: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. Here, n never changes, so the condition stays true and the loop runs forever.
target: A and C both make the loop condition never become false. In A, the body never updates n, so n > 0 stays true forever. The corrective rule is: every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.

source: The if-else statement takes one branch or the other. Here, the else branch runs only when temp > 100 is false, so the program prints boiling for true and not boiling for false.

source: Goal: make the idea of a for loop concrete. Start with the quote: “A for loop iterates over all elements in a container”. source: Worked example from the reading: for i in range(3): print(i) prints 0, 1, 2 — three lines, starting at 0 and stopping before 3. Ask students to predict the next line each iteration (0 then 1 then 2), and point out that the endpoint is not included, so range(3) has exactly three values.

source: Functions & scope mini-review with anchored reminders: show/describe the idea that a function is a named reusable block defined with def, and that variables created inside it are local to that call. source: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second. Therefore names[1] is 'Ben'.
target: “The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.” Ben is the second item, so it’s names[1].

source: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second. The student’s “index 1 is the first element” belief is off by one.
target: The student’s claim is backwards: the first element is at index 0. So lst[1] is the second item, which is 'Ben'.

source: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Since greet() is called between the two print statements, you get “before”, then “hi”, then “after”.
target: “Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().” So 'Hi' prints when greet() is called.

source: A dictionary is the best fit here because it stores key-value pairs and is ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered. Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].
target: Kick off with the core idea of a dictionary: it stores key-value pairs, and you look up values by key (not by numeric position). Show the syntax {key: value} and why dictionaries fit labeled data better than ordered data.

source: Worked example (walkthrough): with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() opens the file, reads all of it into text, and closes it automatically. We’ll also predict what happens if we try to read again in the same file object, and we’ll connect that to the file position advancing through the contents.
target: Worked example grounding with the provided pattern: with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() opens the file, reads all of it into text, and closes it automatically. Show the exact flow: open → read() gets the whole contents as one string → automatic close because of the with statement.

source: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.
target: Reteach core reading concept for students who arrived cold: focus on the position marker. If you call read() twice in a row on the same open file object, the second call returns '' after reaching the end; to read again you must reopen or reset position.

source: Worked example (walkthrough): with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() opens the file, reads all of it into text, and closes it automatically. We’ll also predict what happens if we try to read again in the same file object, and we’ll connect that to the file position advancing through the contents.
target: File I/O worked example: with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() opens the file, reads all of it into text, and closes it automatically. Connect this directly to the ideas: open() returns a file object; read() returns the entire file as a single string; with handles closing.

source: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.
target: Reteach: reading position + end-of-file behavior. Re-center the core concept: read() reads the entire contents into a string; as the file’s position advances, calling read() again at the end returns '' (until reopened or reset). Reinforce the “with” rule to avoid forgetting to close.

source: readlines() returns a list with every line of the file. readline() gives only the next single line, and read() returns the whole file as one string.
target: readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.

source: `readlines()` returns a list containing all the lines in order, which is exactly what the lesson states and what the anchored quote says: “The readlines() function reads the individual lines of a file and returns a string list containing all the lines of the file in order.”
target: The readlines() function reads the individual lines of a file and returns a string list containing all the lines of the file in order.

source: Worked example (from the reading): factorial(n). Walk through the exact logic: factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case), otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call. Trace a couple steps (e.g., n=3) to show the chain of self-calls and where termination happens.
target: Work through factorial as the main example: factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case) and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call. Trace a few calls explicitly (e.g., factorial(3) → factorial(2) → factorial(1) → factorial(0)) to show how the base case stops the chain.

source: Launch recursion: define it using the reading’s framing—“Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem”—and connect it to the mechanics: a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input, continuing until it’s small enough to solve directly (base case). Emphasize the termination requirement: without a base case that stops self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.
target: Reteach the core concept for students who arrived cold using the anchor quotes together: (1) “Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem,” (2) “The recursion process continues until the problem is small enough…,” (3) “without it the calls would never stop.” Then restate the two failure modes: missing base case ⇒ never stops/stack overflow; not shrinking input ⇒ never reaches base case.

source: Recursion is problem reduction: the function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.
target: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem. A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case, where the solution is known or easily found.

source: Worked example (from the reading): the Dog class. Show: class Dog: defines the blueprint; then create a = Dog() and b = Dog(). Connect it directly to attributes: each instance has its own name attribute. Clarify with a quick mental trace: if you change a.name, b.name does not change.
target: Worked example: Dog. Show the idea from the reading’s example: class Dog: defines the blueprint; a = Dog() and b = Dog() are two instances, each with its own name attribute. Then do a quick trace: set a.name to 'Rex' and b.name to 'Milo' and point out that changing one instance’s attributes does not change the other’s; methods are shared.

source: Corrective: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.” Storing per-object data on Dog itself is the confusion.
target: The statement matches the misconception that confuses blueprint with per-object data. The corrective is: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.”

source: Instance attributes are separate per object, so changing one Dog’s name won’t change another Dog’s name. Even though methods are shared from the class, the data each instance carries stays on that instance. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.
target: Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared. The class is the blueprint, not the place where per-object attribute data lives.

source: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. So changing one dog's name does not change the other dog's name; only the methods are shared.
target: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.

source: An economic model simplifies reality by keeping features relevant to the question and discarding others. It is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the problem being studied.
target: Kick off with the economic model idea: an economic model is a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest. Emphasize that simplifying assumptions (e.g., rational choice, perfect competition) generally do not hold exactly, but models are still useful when assumptions are close enough for the question at hand.

source: Perfect-competition predictions mislead in a market dominated by one firm. That is exactly what it means for a model to stop working well: a key assumption breaks, so the model’s conclusions are not reliable there.
target: The worked-example logic is: “Perfect-competition predictions mislead in a market dominated by one firm.” That’s because the model’s assumptions “do not hold exactly,” and it becomes misleading when a key assumption breaks (perfect competition doesn’t hold for that market).

source: An economic model simplifies reality by keeping features relevant to the question and discarding others. It is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the problem being studied.
target: Quick bridge to models: explain why we use simplifying assumptions when reasoning about choices, but we must not treat models as literally true. Keep it tight: an economic model is a simplified representation of reality that discards irrelevant features. Anchor with: “a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest,” and finish with: a model is useful when assumptions are close enough, misleading when a key assumption breaks.

source: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone. The key is differences in opportunity cost, not absolute skill. Trade can raise consumption even when one producer is better at everything.
target: Wrap with the gains-from-trade logic: when each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and trades, “total output rises” and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone. Make students restate the mechanism using opportunity cost language. Connect back to the trade-off definition: resources are limited; choosing more of one means giving up some of another.

source: The model is explicit: the consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint. So the right choice is the affordable bundle with the highest satisfaction, not the most expensive bundle or just any feasible one.
target: Set up consumer choice theory: a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint—so they pick the affordable bundle that yields the highest satisfaction. Emphasize the quote: “selects the affordable bundle of goods that yields the highest satisfaction” and that the choice implies a tradeoff because “utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget.”

source: That mixes up price with cost. The concept says the opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative that must be given up, and a decision that looks free still has an opportunity cost if it uses time or resources that could have produced something else. Always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost.
target: Opportunity cost and trade-offs: define opportunity cost as “the value of the next best alternative that must be given up.” Walk through the rule: rational decision-makers weigh opportunity cost, not just out-of-pocket price. Use the second anchor logic: even “a decision that looks free still has an opportunity cost if it uses time or resources that could have produced something else.”

source: This is the tradeoff idea in the reading: with a fixed budget, buying more concert tickets means buying fewer meals out. At the optimal choice, utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so more of one good requires less of another.
target: This is exactly a tradeoff: “utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget,” so increasing one good (tickets) requires giving up some amount of the other good (meals out).

source: Not quite. The reading defines consumer choice as utility maximization subject to a budget constraint, so the best bundle has to be feasible. In other words, “The optimal bundle is the best one the consumer can actually afford, not the most desirable one.”
target: Corrective: “The optimal bundle is the best one the consumer can actually afford, not the most desirable one.” If a bundle is infeasible due to the budget constraint, it can’t be the optimal choice in utility maximization.

source: “Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand,” meaning higher price is associated with less quantity demanded (holding other factors constant).
target: Primer preview (later lesson) — Demand curve basics, held constant factors, and movements vs shifts. A demand curve shows the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, holding other factors constant. It typically slopes downward (law of demand). A change in price causes movement along the demand curve; a change in income or tastes shifts the curve.

source:
Which formula gives price elasticity of demand?
Change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
Quantity demanded divided by price
Percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
The correct formula is **percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price**. That is the definition used in the lesson, and the absolute value tells us whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
target: Introduce price elasticity of demand as a percentage/percentage idea (not a slope idea). Price elasticity of demand = (percentage change in quantity demanded) / (percentage change in price). Discuss the sign convention informally via absolute value: demand is elastic when the absolute value of elasticity is greater than one; inelastic when it’s less than one. Emphasize we’re measuring responsiveness to price changes.

source:
Which formula gives price elasticity of demand?
Change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
Quantity demanded divided by price
Percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
The correct formula is **percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price**. That is the definition used in the lesson, and the absolute value tells us whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
target: Elasticity is “the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.” Here, |E| = |−5% / 10%| = 0.5, which is less than 1, so demand is inelastic. The key is percentage change in quantity relative to percentage change in price—not absolute units or slope. That directly addresses the common mistake: slope uses absolute units, while elasticity uses percentage changes.

source: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve. The worked example says: “When coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.”
target: Worked example (coffee): “When coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.” Translate that into two distinct moves students must be able to name: (1) a change in price → movement along the same demand curve; (2) more/less buying quantity due to price changes is what causes the downward slope to matter.

source: The law of supply says higher price means higher quantity supplied, so the curve slopes upward. The phrase to keep in mind is that 'a higher price raises the quantity that producers are willing to supply.'
target: Launch: what a supply curve represents (quantity supplied as a flow per period, not a fixed stock). State the law of supply: a higher price raises the quantity producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward. Connect “price → willing to supply” to an upward-sloping curve.

source: This is a move along the supply curve, not a curve shift. The key rule is: 'A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.'
target: The student’s belief confuses move vs shift. The corrective rule is explicit: “A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.” So a price increase means a movement to a higher quantity supplied, not a shift of the whole curve.

source: This matches the worked example logic: “If a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked.” The shortage would normally push the price up, but the ceiling prevents it.
target: Worked example (price ceiling blocked restoring adjustment): If a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked. Walk through it step-by-step: (1) price ceiling keeps the price below the equilibrium price, (2) at that lower price quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (shortage), (3) the market would normally be pushed upward by the shortage, but the ceiling blocks that restoring price rise—so the shortage persists.

source: Not so: equilibrium is when "the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change." That is a stable price, not a frozen market.
target: Reteach the core misconception: equilibrium is not a frozen market. Re-state the equilibrium quote ideas in plain language: equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not “nothing happens.” Use a fast re-explanation of shortage/surplus push directions and how equilibrium eliminates the *tendency* for price to change.

source: Not so: equilibrium is when "the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change." That is a stable price, not a frozen market.
target: Correct the misconception directly: “Equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.” The point of equilibrium is that the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied, so there is “no tendency for the price to change,” even though buying and selling still occur.

source: Use the rule: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve.” So when coffee’s own price rises, that is movement along the supply curve (higher quantity supplied).
target: Confront the key rule: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.” A higher coffee price changes quantity supplied (movement along the curve), not the curve itself.

source: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve. The worked example says: “When coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.”
target: The correct matching is: price change → movement along the curve. The demand example says: “When coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.” Shifts come from non-price factors (income, tastes), not from the good’s own price.

source: Not so: equilibrium is when "the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change." That is a stable price, not a frozen market.
target: Equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market. Even when buying and selling continue, the demand and supply pressures offset each other so the price has no tendency to change.

source: Correcting an externality means making decision-makers face costs the market boundary leaves out. That reduces overproduction caused by prices that ignore spillover harm.
target: When costs (or benefits) fall on a third party not part of the exchange, the market boundary leaves them out. For a negative externality, that means the market price excludes the spillover cost and the market produces more than the socially efficient quantity. The correction is to make decision-makers face the costs the market boundary leaves out.

source: A monopoly is “a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.” The key terms are single seller, no close substitutes, and barriers to entry.
target: Monopoly and market power: define monopoly as “a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.” Emphasize the price-maker difference: unlike a price-taking competitive firm, a monopoly can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells. Preview what students will do: connect that idea to why monopoly creates deadweight loss.

source: Not so: equilibrium is when "the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change." That is a stable price, not a frozen market.
target: Reteach for students who arrived cold (core concept): Market equilibrium is not “frozen.” Quote the definition: “the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers,” and then add: “the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change.” Use one quick equilibrium check: surplus pushes price down; shortage pushes it up.

source: Not so: equilibrium is when "the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change." That is a stable price, not a frozen market.
target: Equilibrium is “a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.” At the equilibrium price, the opposing pressures are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change.

source: The circular flow says money returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out as saving, taxes, or imports. But leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports. Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.
target: Set the frame: circular flow is a loop of spending and income. Emphasize the key rule from the reading: “money that households earn returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out of the flow as saving, taxes, or spending on imports.” Define: households earn income → spend → firms receive → firms pay households.

source: Your choice should match the worked example: “Household saving deposited in a bank is lent to firms as investment, re-injecting money that had leaked out of the flow.” So saving is a leakage, but investment re-injects the spending back into the circular flow.
target: Worked example (bank/investment chain): Household saving deposited in a bank is lent to firms as investment, re-injecting money that had leaked out of the flow. Use it to map: saving = leakage; investment = injection; the flow balances when leakages are matched by injections.

source:
In the circular flow of income, leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports. Which outcome matches this balance condition?
Total leakages exceed total injections, so national income rises
Total leakages exceed total injections, so national income falls
Total leakages equal total injections, so national income neither rises nor falls
Total leakages equal total injections, so national income rises
Using the anchor condition: "When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls." That’s exactly the third option.
target: Teach equilibrium in the flow (balance, not “growth” by default): “Leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports that add spending back into the flow.” Then connect to national income: “When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls.”

source: Confronting the misconception: "Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports." In the circular flow, saving is a leakage, but it must be matched by injections like investment, government spending, and exports when the economy is in balance.
target: Reteach the core concept for anyone who arrived cold: saving is not “gone”; it’s a leakage only if we don’t match it with injections. Restate corrective explicitly using the reading’s logic: saving must be matched by investment (or government spending/exports as applicable) to keep the circular flow in balance.

source: Confronting the misconception: "Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports." In the circular flow, saving is a leakage, but it must be matched by injections like investment, government spending, and exports when the economy is in balance.
target: Corrective to the misconception: “Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.” In the circular flow, higher saving is a leakage that must be balanced by injections to keep income stable.

source: This is directly tied to the definition: capital stock "rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation." Also, capital stock is a LEVEL (total equipment/structures/tools), not the flow of investment per year.
target: Teach c-20/c-21: Define capital stock and capital accumulation. Capital stock = total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools. It “rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation.” Net investment = gross investment minus depreciation, and it is “the change in the capital stock over a period.” Key rule: “the stock grows only when net investment is positive.”

source: This targets the level-vs-flow mistake. The corrective is: "Higher investment raises the stock gradually over time; the stock does not jump when the flow changes." Investment is a flow; the capital stock responds over time through net investment.
target: Worked example (anchor): Imagine a factory’s machinery “builds up over years of net investment; one year of higher spending nudges the trajectory, it does not double the stock overnight.” Use this to correct the level-vs-flow mistake: if investment rises this year, the capital stock does not instant-jump; it changes gradually over time as net investment is positive year after year.

source: Net investment is “gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.” That is the key relationship to use when deciding whether the stock rises or falls.
target: Net investment is the driver of the change in the capital stock: "gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period." If net investment stays at −$5 million, the capital stock declines by the same amount in Year 2 as in Year 1, even if gross investment was higher.

source: People who have given up looking are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed. That is why “recount the rate including discouraged workers and ask whose situation each definition makes visible” matters: the measured unemployment rate can look lower when discouraged workers are excluded.
target: Worked example from the reading idea: “In a weak job market the official rate can fall simply because discouraged workers stop looking and drop out of the labor force.” Step through: if workers become discouraged and stop searching, they move from the labor force to out of the labor force, so the measured unemployment rate can drop even though joblessness is still “felt.” Quote in-class to anchor: “people who have given up looking are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed.”

source:
A person stopped searching after months of rejection and is no longer looking for work. In the official labor statistics, how is this person counted?
Employed
Unemployed
Out of the labor force
Frictionally unemployed
People who have given up looking are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed. That is why “recount the rate including discouraged workers and ask whose situation each definition makes visible” matters: the measured unemployment rate can look lower when discouraged workers are excluded.
target: Unemployment is measured as people who are without a job, are available for work, and are actively searching for work (not including those not in the labor force). Marco has given up looking, so he is classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed. That matters because the labor-force boundary can make the official rate look neutral while excluding discouraged workers by choice; to understand the situation fully, recount the rate including discouraged workers and ask whose experience each definition makes visible.

source: Not quite. The reading defines consumer choice as utility maximization subject to a budget constraint, so the best bundle has to be feasible. In other words, “The optimal bundle is the best one the consumer can actually afford, not the most desirable one.”
target: The corrective language is: “The optimal bundle is the best one the consumer can actually afford, not the most desirable one.” In consumer choice theory, utility maximization is subject to the budget constraint, so infeasible (unaffordable) bundles can’t be optimal.

source: The asthenosphere is in the upper mantle. It is “solid rock that flows slowly by convection,” driven by heat from the core. That slow flow can transfer motion to the rigid plates above (not by melting into a liquid magma ocean).
target: Worked example (anchor the mechanism): Use the quote and analogy: “this layer moves and flows due to convection currents created by heat coming from the earth's core.” Then connect directly to the mantle/astenosphere idea: mantle convection moves hot rock like slow-boiling soup over millions of years, dragging rigid plates above it — no liquid magma layer required. Emphasize: asthenosphere is solid rock, mechanically weak, flows slowly by convection (not a magma ocean).

source: This is one of the key corrections for today: “The core has both a liquid outer layer and a solid inner layer; the inner core is solid despite being hotter, because the immense pressure keeps the iron solid.”
target: Core structure emphasis: Teach the two-layer core idea carefully: “The core of the Earth has both liquid and solid layers and consists mostly of iron, nickel…” Then address the temperature vs state misconception: inner core is solid even though hotter, because immense pressure keeps the iron solid.

source: The reading states: “The core has both a liquid outer layer and a solid inner layer.” So the core is not all molten.
target: This addresses the misconception you’ll often hear: “Students assume the whole core is molten.” The corrective from the reading is: “The core has both a liquid outer layer and a solid inner layer; the inner core is solid despite being hotter, because the immense pressure keeps the iron solid.”

source: The core is made mostly of iron and nickel, and it has both liquid and solid layers. The crust is the outermost layer, and the asthenosphere is part of the mantle.
target: The reading says the asthenosphere is “solid rock” and “mechanically weak,” flowing slowly by convection. It also says the core has “both liquid and solid layers” and is “made mostly of iron and nickel.”

source: The asthenosphere is in the upper mantle. It is “solid rock that flows slowly by convection,” driven by heat from the core. That slow flow can transfer motion to the rigid plates above (not by melting into a liquid magma ocean).
target: The worked example states: “Mantle convection moves hot rock like slow-boiling soup over millions of years, dragging the rigid plates above it — no liquid magma layer required.” This aligns with the corrective: asthenosphere is “solid rock” that flows slowly by convection, not magma ocean flow.

source: Use streak: "Streak examines the color of a powdered mineral." In the hematite example, hematite can look silvery or red, but its streak is always reddish-brown—"the powder color gives it away when the specimen color does not."
target: Worked example anchor: Hematite. Emphasize the misconception trap with color vs. streak: “Hematite can look silvery or red, but its streak is always reddish-brown — the powder color gives it away when the specimen color does not.” Show how you would identify it by testing streak rather than trusting surface color.

source: Follow the corrective: "Color is unreliable; streak (the color of the powder) and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably." Streak directly tests powder color rather than surface appearance.
target: This matches the corrective: “Color is unreliable; streak (the color of the powder) and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably.” Streak is designed to be consistent even when surface color varies.

source: Corrective: “Hardness measures scratch resistance, not toughness; diamond tops the Mohs scale yet has perfect cleavage and can be split by a sharp blow along those planes.” A mineral can be very hard but still break along cleavage.
target: Directly correct the misconception: “Hardness measures scratch resistance, not toughness; diamond tops the Mohs scale yet has perfect cleavage and can be split by a sharp blow along those planes.” Mohs hardness is about scratching behavior, not how it breaks under impacts.

source: Cleavage is "the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding." If minerals without such planes fracture irregularly, then regular flat break lines point to cleavage.
target: Cleavage is defined exactly as: “the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding; minerals without such planes fracture irregularly.” Your flat-plane observation is the key indicator.

source: Follow the corrective: "Color is unreliable; streak (the color of the powder) and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably." Streak directly tests powder color rather than surface appearance.
target: Confront the misconception directly: “Color is unreliable; streak (the color of the powder) and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably.” The key fix is to use streak and other diagnostic physical properties rather than trusting surface appearance.

source: It is a three-dimensional shape — one silicon at the center surrounded by four oxygens at the corners of a tetrahedron, not a flat triangle. Choose the option that states the tetrahedron is 3-D with four corner oxygens.
target: Correct the misconception directly: “It is a three-dimensional shape — one silicon at the center surrounded by four oxygens at the corners of a tetrahedron, not a flat triangle.” The SiO4 unit is built in 3-D even if paper diagrams simplify it.

source: More shared corner oxygens means a more interconnected framework; quartz, a fully linked framework silicate, is among the harder, more durable minerals. Greater linkage strengthens the framework instead of weakening it.
target: Confront the misconception: “More shared corner oxygens means a more interconnected framework; quartz, a fully linked framework silicate, is among the harder, more durable minerals.” In other words, increasing linkage (more shared corner oxygen) leads to stronger, more durable behavior in the context given.

source: The chain is: “High viscosity means a thick and sticky magma… that flows slowly,” which traps gas until it erupts violently. The most dangerous volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow (fast cloud of hot ash and gas) typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes.
target: Volcanism: eruptive style from viscosity (silica controls viscosity). Use the anchor: “Silica content controls magma viscosity and the eruptive style of volcanoes.” Contrast two end-members: low-silica, low-viscosity basaltic magma flows easily like syrup → gentle eruptions (e.g., Hawaiian shield volcanoes). High-silica, high-viscosity magma is thick and sticky like toothpaste → traps gas until it erupts explosively. source:
A student says Earth formed only a few million years ago, so human history and dinosaurs nearly overlap. Which correction best fits geologic time?
Earth is 4.54 billion years old.
Earth is about 10,000 years old.

(2) Relative dating still does not give numerical years: remind them that relative dating only orders events as older/younger, while numerical ages in years come from absolute dating methods such as radiometric dating.
