source: You need two complete comparisons joined by and. Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: age > 13 and age < 19. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left.
target: You need two comparisons joined by and. The correct condition is: age > 13 and age < 19. The and operator returns True only if both conditions are true, so the body runs only in that range. The version 'age > 13 and < 19' is wrong because the bare '< 19' has nothing on its left.

source: The else branch runs only when the if condition is false. Since temp > 100 is false when temp is 100, it prints `not boiling`.
target: If the condition is true, the body is executed; if the condition is false, the body is not executed. Here temp > 100 is false, so the else branch runs and prints 'not boiling'.

source: Termination depends on making progress toward ending the loop expression. Corrective: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” If the condition never becomes false, the loop can be infinite.
target: Start with the core idea: a while loop repeatedly runs its loop body while the loop expression stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration. Anchor on the idea that once the loop statement executes, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue. Emphasize: termination happens when the condition becomes false; if it never becomes false, you get an infinite loop—so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.

source: Worked example re-teach (from the reading): “n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1 prints 3, 2, 1 and then stops when n reaches 0.” Walk the trace step-by-step: show each time you evaluate the loop condition, then execute the body, then update n, then re-check the condition again. Anchor with: “At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again.”
target: Worked example from the reading: n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1 prints 3, 2, 1 and then stops when n reaches 0. Walk the cycle: (1) check n > 0, (2) run body, (3) update n = n - 1, (4) re-evaluate the loop expression at the top of the next iteration. Point to the anchor quote: “At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again”.

source: Corrective: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” Without updating, the loop can run forever (an infinite loop).
target: Corrective applied directly: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” Option 3 updates n downward, so n > 0 eventually becomes false.

source: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. Here, the loop starts because n < 3 is true (n=1), then the body runs and prints 2; next iteration condition is checked again (2 < 3) so it runs and prints 3; then 3 < 3 is false and the loop ends.
target: The corrective is: “The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.” So the condition n < 3 is true for the first iteration, the body runs and prints 3, and only after that does the loop expression get evaluated again; then 3 < 3 is false, so it stops.

source: Introduce for loops. Emphasize the key mental model: a for loop iterates over all elements in a container, binding a loop variable to one element at a time (the container can be a range, a string, or a list). Then connect to range(): range() produces a sequence of integers, and range(n) yields 0 through n-1. Walk through what that means for counting: if you want 3 iterations, you iterate over range(3) to get 0, 1, 2.
target: Introduce for loops + range: “A for loop iterates over all elements in a container.” Define container types used here: range of numbers, string, list. Explain range specifically with the anchor quote “The range() function produces a sequence of integers” and the key rule range(n) yields 0 through n-1. Show: for i in range(3): print(i) prints 0, 1, 2.

source: Corrective: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” Without updating, the loop can run forever (an infinite loop).
target: Confronting the belief: "The condition will become false later automatically even if I don't change n." That is wrong. Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; here n is never updated, so n > 0 stays true forever and the loop becomes an infinite loop.

source: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. So the loop prints those five integers in order.
target: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. So i takes those five values and the loop prints 0 1 2 3 4.

source: The condition is checked only at the top of each iteration, so both print statements in the body run before the next test. The loop does not re-check the condition the instant `n` changes.
target: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration. Changing n inside the body does not interrupt the current pass; the rest of the body still runs before the condition is checked again. So print(n) is not skipped in that iteration.

source: Hook: remind students that a function is “a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called.” Show the standard shape: def name(params): then an indented body. Emphasize when it runs: only when you call it by name. Use the anchor idea: defining a function stores it; calling it runs the body.
target: Hook + core idea: functions as named, reusable blocks. Read/produce the function pattern: def name(...): then an indented body. Stress the “runs only when called” behavior using square(). Anchor with: “A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called” and “A function is defined using the def keyword.”

source: We walk through the worked example: def square(n): return n * n. Point out: (1) def square(n): defines a reusable calculation, (2) the body runs when square(5) is called, and (3) it returns 25. Then quickly add scope reasoning: a variable created inside square would be local to that call; the only thing the rest of the program reliably gets is what the function returns.
target:
Worked example (scope + return):
def square(n):
    return n * n

Then call: square(5) -> 25. Point out what runs during definition vs during the call. Immediately connect to scope: variables created inside the call are local to that call. Use this anchor quote: “A variable created within a function has local scope and only exists within the function.”

source: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range. For a 5-item list, valid positions are 0 through 4, so the last element is lst[4].
target: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; names[4] is the last element, 'El'.

source: Warm-up: contrast lists vs dictionaries by “how you find a value.” Show the key idea: a dictionary stores key→value pairs and you look up values by key, not by numeric position. Anchor with the reading’s idea: “A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs”.
target: Warm-up + goal for the lesson: dictionaries store key-value pairs and look up values by key (not numeric position). Anchor with the idea: “A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs.” Show basic dictionary syntax with curly braces in key: value form.

source: A dictionary is not read by numeric position. It is accessed by key, so `grades['Ava']` returns the value stored under the key `'Ava'`. The corrective is: “Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].”
target: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0]. Here, use grades['Ava'] to get the 95 stored under 'Ava'.

source:
For s = 'Python', what does s[0:3] return?
'Pyt'
'Pyth'
'Pytho'
'Python'
The end index of a slice is exclusive, so s[0:3] returns characters at indices 0, 1, and 2 — three characters, stopping before index 3.
target: The end index of a slice is exclusive, so s[0:3] returns characters at indices 0, 1, and 2 — three characters, stopping before index 3. For 'Python', that is 'Pyt'.

source: Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: `age > 13 and age < 19`. The bare `< 19` has nothing on its left, so `if age > 13 and < 19:` is not valid.
target: Use two full comparisons joined by `and`: `age > 13 and age < 19`. The bare `< 19` has nothing on its left, so `age > 13 and < 19` is not a valid compound condition.

source: Convert the number with `str()` before joining it to text, or use formatting. Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a `+` with a `str`, so `'Age: ' + 19` raises a type error.
target: Convert the number with `str()` before joining it to text, or use formatting. Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a `+` with a `str`, so `'Age: ' + 19` raises a TypeError.

source: The student is applying math-equality thinking. The corrective is: “In Python = is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one.”
target: Have students internalize this corrective: In Python `= is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one.

source: Launch recursion: define it using the reading’s framing—“Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem”—and connect it to the mechanics: a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input, continuing until it’s small enough to solve directly (base case). Emphasize the termination requirement: without a base case that stops self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.
target: Warm-up re-teach: define recursion using the anchor idea: “Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem”. We map the parts: recursive case = call itself on a smaller input; base case = simplest input solved directly; termination = base case eventually reached.

source: This is the worked-example structure: factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case) and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call. That shrink is what ensures you eventually reach the base case.
target: Worked example (factorial): show factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case) and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call. Emphasize two checks every time: (1) Where is the base case? (2) What expression makes progress toward it (like n - 1)? Tie to the quote “without it the calls would never stop”.

source: Bridge from functions to recursion. Review: functions are defined with def and run only when called. Connect to recursion: a recursive function is just a function that—when called—calls itself. Then highlight scope during recursion: variables created inside a function are local to that call; if you need a value outside, you return it. (We’ll use this during tracing.)
target: Connect recursion to scope/return values and function calling. Review the function rule: defining with def only stores the code; it runs when called by name. Then address local variables: values created inside a function don’t exist outside that call; to use them later, the function must return the result and the caller must capture it.

source: The issue is that each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1). As the corrective states: “Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.”
target: You confront the misconception directly: “Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.” If the recursive call uses the same n, the process can repeat forever and never solve the simpler version.

source: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. In this code, y is local to square(). The value from return y only becomes available outside if you store it (for example, result = square(5)).
target: This matches the local-scope rule: “Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.” Here, you correctly capture with result = square(5), but temp is not available outside the call.

source: Fix this misconception: “Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().”
target: Correct the timing misconception: “Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().” So you need greet() to run the body.

source: A class is the blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
target: Warm start: contrast “blueprint” vs “thing built from it.” We’ll use the core anchor ideas: a class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it’s a blueprint; objects built from it are instances. Show the anchor quotes on screen: “A class is a blueprint for creating objects” and “Individual objects created of the class type are called instances.”

source: `a = Dog()` and `b = Dog()` create two instances from the class blueprint. The worked example says each instance has its own `name` attribute. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.
target: Worked example (Dog): Start with the provided code idea: class Dog: defines the blueprint; a = Dog() and b = Dog() are two instances, each with its own name attribute. Explain what “own copy of the attributes” means: if a.name and b.name exist as attributes on the instances, then changing a.name does not change b.name. Emphasize what is shared: the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

source: The class is the blueprint, and the pet you build from it is the instance. Attributes belong to each instance, while the class supplies shared methods. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.
target: You should confront this directly: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.” The class defines attributes/methods as a type; the instances hold the per-object attribute values.

source: Correct: “Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.” Attribute data is per instance; methods are shared across instances.
target: Direct correction: “Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.” Sharing applies to the methods defined in the class, not to each instance’s attribute data.

source: The last position in a 5-item list is index 4, not 5. “Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence,” so a 5-item list's last index is 4; `names[5]` is out of range and raises an error.
target: The fix comes from reading the failure and applying index rules: “Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range.” If the list has length 5, valid indexes are 0..4, so `names[4]` is the last element.

source: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Here message is local to make_message, so print(message) outside the function cannot read it. Returning the string is the correct repair. Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().
target: The issue is scope: “Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.” So you should `return message` and then assign `m = greet()` before printing.

source: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Simply defining it does not execute the body.
target: The correction is direct: “Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().” Defs don’t execute the body until you call the function.

source: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset. So a gets the full contents, and b becomes an empty string.
target: This targets the reading position marker: “Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.” So the first `read()` gets all content, the second gets an empty string, and `a == b` is False.

source: Option 2 is correct because it both (a) uses the right loop expression (n > 0) and (b) updates the variable so the condition eventually becomes false: n = n - 1. This satisfies the while-loop requirement that the loop body make progress toward ending the condition.
target: Correct choice B because inside the loop body you update the variable used in the loop condition. Every while loop must make progress toward ending the condition; a counter loop needs `n = n - 1` so eventually the condition `n > 0` becomes false and the loop terminates.

source: Correct. This directly addresses the misconception: “The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.” So if the body changes n, the change won’t prevent the *current* pass from finishing—it affects the decision for the *next* iteration.
target: This directly contradicts the misconception. Clarify that the loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. Changes inside the body affect whether the next iteration will run, not the remainder of the current one.

source: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length, so a 3-item list’s last index is 2. names[2] returns 'Cy', while names[5] is out of range. The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.
target: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence. For a 3-item list, valid indices are 0, 1, 2, so `names[2]` is the third item: 'Cy'.

source: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use `d['name']` to get the value stored under the key `'name'`, not `d[0]`. If you want Ava's score, ask for the key `'Ava'` directly.
target: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use `d['name']` to get the value stored under the key 'name', not `d[0]`. In this example, the key to look up for Ava is `'Ava'`, not 0.

source: Confronting the misconception: “Students write a recursive function with no base case, so it recurses forever.” The corrective is: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.”
target: Confronting the misconception: “Students write a recursive function with no base case, so it recurses forever and raises a RecursionError.” Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.

source: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. So changing one dog's name does not change the other dog's name; only the methods are shared.
target: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. `d = Dog()`), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. If both dogs’ `name` changes together, that points to confusing the class with its instances or storing data in the wrong place.

source: This addresses the misconception head-on. The corrective in the lesson is: “A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.” If assumptions clearly fail, the model’s conclusions can mislead—so you do not apply it as if it were literally true.
target: Use the corrective: “A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.” If rational choice clearly fails, the model’s conclusions are not dependable for the question at hand.

source: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises. That extra output is what makes it possible for both sides to consume beyond what they could produce alone.
target: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, “total output rises.” This is exactly the comparative-advantage mechanism: gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not absolute skill. So total output rises even if neither producer is best at everything.

source:
Which formula gives price elasticity of demand?
Change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
Quantity demanded divided by price
Percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
The correct formula is **percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price**. That is the definition used in the lesson, and the absolute value tells us whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
target: Introduce price elasticity of demand (PED). Define it as “the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.” Then translate the definition into the elastic/inelastic decision rule: demand is elastic when the absolute value of elasticity is greater than one. Connect responsiveness to price changes with the idea of substitutability: close substitutes make demand more elastic; necessities tend to be inelastic because consumers have few substitutes.

source: Yes—this matches both kernel ideas and the anchor. The course states: “Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes,” and also “The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity.” That’s exactly the insulin logic in the worked example.
target: Worked example with insulin (anchor): “Insulin has highly inelastic demand because patients have no close substitute.” Ask students: if price rises, would quantity demanded change a lot or a little, relative to the price change? Tie the story back to the kernel logic: few substitutes → consumers can’t switch easily → elasticity is low (|elasticity| < 1).

source:
Which formula gives price elasticity of demand?
Change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
Quantity demanded divided by price
Percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
The correct formula is **percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price**. That is the definition used in the lesson, and the absolute value tells us whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
target: Start with the demand-curve fact: “A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve.” Then use elasticity’s definition: elasticity is “the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.” That means elasticity classification is about percentage changes, not about slope in absolute units.

source: “Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand,” meaning higher price is associated with less quantity demanded (holding other factors constant).
target: Set up the demand curve: remind students what a demand curve measures (quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, holding other factors constant). Use the quote to anchor: “the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding all other factors constant.” Show a downward slope as reflecting the law of demand.

source:
Which formula gives price elasticity of demand?
Change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
Quantity demanded divided by price
Percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
The correct formula is **percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price**. That is the definition used in the lesson, and the absolute value tells us whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
target: Transition to demand elasticity only as needed for intuition: define price elasticity of demand as “the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.” Connect to elasticity vs inelasticity using the percentage-change logic (not slope): elastic vs inelastic depends on whether |elasticity| is greater or less than 1.

source: This is a price change, so it causes a movement along the demand curve. The coffee example says that when coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.
target: A “change in price causes a movement along the demand curve,” not a shift. When the coffee price falls, consumers buy more coffee—so you move down along the curve and quantity demanded increases.

source: The law of supply says higher price means higher quantity supplied, so the curve slopes upward. The phrase to keep in mind is that 'a higher price raises the quantity that producers are willing to supply.'
target: Present the law of supply and the upward slope. Use the anchor quote: “a higher price raises the quantity that producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward.” Emphasize what is plotted: price of the good (on the vertical axis) vs. quantity supplied (per period).

source: Correct: a higher price “raises the quantity producers are willing to supply,” which means this is a move along the supply curve (not a shift). The anchor idea is: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.”
target: A price change moves you along the existing supply curve: the price of the good changes the quantity producers are willing to supply. This matches the idea that “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve.” A shift requires a non-price factor like input costs or technology.

source: A frost is a non-price factor affecting production, so it changes supply at every price. That is why it shifts the whole curve. This matches the corrective rule: only non-price factors shift the curve, while “A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.”
target: A frost that kills plants changes production possibilities, so supply changes at every price. That is why it “shifts the whole curve” rather than causing a move along it. The anchor rule is: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve.”

source: Correct: a higher price “raises the quantity producers are willing to supply,” which means this is a move along the supply curve (not a shift). The anchor idea is: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.”
target: False. Under the law of supply, higher price increases the quantity producers are willing to supply, which means you move along the supply curve. Only non-price factors shift the curve. Use the anchor: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve.”

source: Input costs are a non-price factor, so they shift the entire supply curve. The supply-curve rule you need is: “A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.” Therefore, higher input costs (non-price) shift the curve (typically left).
target: Rising input costs are a non-price factor. Non-price factors shift the whole supply curve, not just the quantity at a specific price. The anchor statement guides the classification: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve.”

source: This matches the worked example logic: “If a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked.” The shortage would normally push the price up, but the ceiling prevents it.
target: Worked-example: price ceiling. Scenario: If a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked. Have students trace the logic in two steps: (1) at the ceiling price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied → shortage; (2) without the ability for price to rise toward equilibrium, the “push” back toward equilibrium can’t happen, so the shortage persists.

source: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so a surplus appears. As the reading says, "a surplus pushes it down"; the price falls toward equilibrium.
target: Correct: at a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus that “pushes it down.” At a price below equilibrium, the restoring force goes the other way (shortage pushes up).

source: Input costs are a non-price factor, so they shift the entire supply curve. The supply-curve rule you need is: “A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.” Therefore, higher input costs (non-price) shift the curve (typically left).
target: Input costs are a non-price factor, so they shift the supply curve. A higher cost reduces the quantity producers are willing to supply at each price, so the supply curve shifts left (not a movement along caused by a change in the good’s own price).

source: This is a move along the supply curve, not a curve shift. The key rule is: 'A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.'
target: Correct. The statement matches the rule: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.” So an own-price increase leads to a move along supply (not a shift).

source: This is a move along the supply curve, not a curve shift. The key rule is: 'A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.'
target: For supply, this is the distinction you must use: “A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.” So you get a movement along supply, not a full curve shift.

source: A monopoly is “a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.” The key terms are single seller, no close substitutes, and barriers to entry.
target: Quick launch: define monopoly using the reading’s exact kernel idea: “a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.” Emphasize the contrast with competition: a monopoly is a price maker, not a price taker.

source: Correct choice is the demand-curve constraint: “A monopoly is constrained by the demand curve: to raise price it must sell less.” A price maker can choose a higher price, but that choice only works with a lower quantity demanded.
target: Correct: “A monopoly is constrained by the demand curve: to raise price it must sell less.” Even with no close substitutes, the quantity demanded falls when price rises.

source: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so a surplus appears. As the reading says, "a surplus pushes it down"; the price falls toward equilibrium.
target: With a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (a surplus). The kernel fact says: “a surplus pushes it down.” Equilibrium is about restoring pressures, not a frozen market.

source: Correct choice is the demand-curve constraint: “A monopoly is constrained by the demand curve: to raise price it must sell less.” A price maker can choose a higher price, but that choice only works with a lower quantity demanded.
target: Direct correction: “A monopoly is constrained by the demand curve: to raise price it must sell less.” Higher prices reduce the quantity buyers are willing to purchase.

source: This matches the worked example logic: “If a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked.” The shortage would normally push the price up, but the ceiling prevents it.
target: This matches the worked-example logic: “If a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked.” The ceiling prevents the adjustment back toward equilibrium.

source: The circular flow says money returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out as saving, taxes, or imports. But leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports. Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.
target: Set up the circular flow story in plain terms: households earn money and then it returns to firms as spending. Emphasize the “unless” part—some of that money leaks out as saving, taxes, or spending on imports. Quote from the reading: “money that households earn returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out of the flow as saving, taxes, or spending on imports.”

source: Your choice should match the worked example: “Household saving deposited in a bank is lent to firms as investment, re-injecting money that had leaked out of the flow.” So saving is a leakage, but investment re-injects the spending back into the circular flow.
target: Worked example (use the provided one): “Household saving deposited in a bank is lent to firms as investment, re-injecting money that had leaked out of the flow.” Connect the dots explicitly: saving is a leakage, but it doesn’t vanish—when matched by investment, the circular flow continues. Tie back to the balance condition: quote “When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls.”

source: Saving is a leakage, but it is not destroyed. The corrective is exactly that: “Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.” The circular flow stays balanced when leakages are matched by injections.
target: This confronts the misconception directly. The corrective is: “Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.” In the circular flow, saving is a leakage that can be balanced by injections.

source: Use the core balance condition: “Leakages are balanced by injections… When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance.” If leakages rise (more saving) but injections don’t, total leakages ≠ total injections, so the flow is not in balance.
target: The kernel fact states the balance condition: “When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance.” So the correct matching idea is injections to leakages so that their totals are equal.

source: Net investment is “gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.” That is the key relationship to use when deciding whether the stock rises or falls.
target: Connect net investment to the sign rule: “the stock grows only when net investment is positive.” Then do a quick scenario check: if depreciation is high enough that gross investment minus depreciation is negative, the capital stock falls. Tie this back to definitions: net investment is the change in the capital stock over a period.

source: That belief confuses the level with the flow. Higher investment raises the stock gradually over time; the stock does not jump when the flow changes. The factory example makes the same point: one year of higher spending nudges the trajectory, it does not double the stock overnight.

Higher investment raises the stock gradually over time; the stock does not jump when the flow changes.

source: Net investment is “gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.” That is the key relationship to use when deciding whether the stock rises or falls.
target: Net investment is “gross investment minus depreciation,” and that is “the change in the capital stock over a period.” Remember: the capital stock is a level, while net investment is a flow that changes the level.

source: Confronting the misconception: "Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports." In the circular flow, saving is a leakage, but it must be matched by injections like investment, government spending, and exports when the economy is in balance.
target: This corrects the misconception that “saving disappears from the economy.” The model says money leaks out of the flow as “saving, taxes, or spending on imports,” and “Leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports.” In balance, the circular flow works out so income neither rises nor falls.

source: People who have given up looking are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed. target: This is exactly the boundary problem: “discouraged workers who are excluded make unemployment look lower than the felt experience of joblessness.” If discouraged workers stop looking, they are “classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed,” so the official unemployment rate can fall even if true joblessness hasn’t improved.

source: This is the point of model use: 'A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.' When a key assumption breaks, the model can mislead.
target: Corrective: “A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.” If a key assumption breaks, the model can mislead—even if the model is useful in other contexts.

source: Not so: equilibrium is when "the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change." That is a stable price, not a frozen market.
target: Corrective: “Equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.” The point is that demand and supply pressures offset, so price has no tendency to change.

source: The asthenosphere is in the upper mantle. It is “solid rock that flows slowly by convection,” driven by heat from the core. That slow flow can transfer motion to the rigid plates above (not by melting into a liquid magma ocean).
target: Focus on the mantle’s state and how it moves. Teach: upper mantle asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection; it is mechanically weak but not a magma ocean. Use the worked-example idea: hot rock rises, cooler rock sinks, and that slow motion can drag the rigid plates above it. Quote/ground: “this layer moves and flows due to convection currents created by heat coming from the earth's core.”

source: The worked example leads to streak: hematite can look silvery or red, but its streak is always reddish-brown, so the powder color gives it away when the specimen color does not.
target: Work hematite as a color-vs-streak example. Show/describe: hematite can look silvery or red, but its streak is always reddish-brown—"the powder color gives it away when the specimen color does not." Use this to introduce the idea that streak is more reliable than specimen color.

source:
Two igneous rocks have similar chemistry. One has large crystals and the other has tiny crystals. What explains the difference best?
The large-crystal rock cooled fast at the surface
The tiny-crystal rock cooled slowly at depth
The large-crystal rock cooled slowly at depth
Crystal size only depends on whether the rock is sedimentary
Slow cooling at depth gives crystals time to grow large (coarse, intrusive); fast cooling at the surface freezes tiny crystals (fine, extrusive).
target: Start with the anchor idea for igneous rocks: “Igneous rock is formed when liquid rock freezes into a solid rock.” Connect magma vs lava, then jump to cooling rate → texture: slow cooling at depth gives large crystals (intrusive/coarse); fast cooling at the surface gives tiny crystals (extrusive/fine). Use granite vs basalt as the quick comparison: same general chemistry possible, but different crystal size because of cooling rate.

source: Magma is molten rock below the surface; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava, and the two cool at very different rates. Keep the location in mind first, because that is what separates the terms.
target: Magma is molten rock below the surface; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava, and the two cool at very different rates. So the correct distinction is molten below the surface (magma) vs molten on the surface after eruption (lava).

source: It is the opposite: cooler, silica-rich, high-viscosity magma traps gas and produces the deadliest pyroclastic eruptions, whereas runny basalt usually erupts effusively. That explosive setting points straight to pyroclastic flow.
target: It is the opposite: cooler, silica-rich, high-viscosity magma traps gas and produces the deadliest pyroclastic eruptions, whereas runny basalt usually erupts effusively. So the correct response is option 2.

source: More shared corner oxygens means a more interconnected framework; quartz, a fully linked framework silicate, is among the harder, more durable minerals. Greater linkage strengthens the framework instead of weakening it.
target: More shared corner oxygens means a more interconnected framework; quartz, a fully linked framework silicate, is among the harder, more durable minerals. So option 2 is the best correction.

source: Corrective: “Each layer's grain size, sorting, and fossils record a specific past environment — a river, beach, or deep sea — so layers are evidence, not decoration.” Use those features to reconstruct depositional conditions.
target: Feature-to-environment quick sort. Give 4 short rock-feature descriptions (no calculations): one with coarse grains + cross/ripple texture; one with fine-grained layers + marine fossils; one described as poorly sorted with mixed grain sizes; one described as well-sorted sand. Students choose the depositional environment (river, beach/current-swept shallow marine, deep sea quiet water). They must justify using at least one: grain size/sorting and/or fossils. Instructor circulates and calls out evidence vs decoration: “Each layer's grain size, sorting, and fossils record a specific past environment — a river, beach, or deep sea — so layers are evidence, not decoration.”

source: The cycle has many paths: any rock type can become any other; metamorphic rock can erode to sediment, or melt to magma and re-crystallize as igneous rock. Over geologic time the same atoms cycle repeatedly through igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic forms as conditions change.
target: Rock cycle flexibility (c-13): Teach it as a system with many paths, not a single one-way arrow. Use the anchor quote: “describes the major materials that comprise the Earth, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.” Explicitly contrast: (1) if rocks melt to magma, that restarts with new igneous rocks; (2) metamorphic products can erode to sediment; (3) over geologic time, the same atoms cycle through all three families.

source: Over geologic time the same atoms cycle repeatedly through igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic forms. The rock cycle shows rocks continually transform as conditions change.
target: The correct idea is: “Over geologic time the same atoms cycle repeatedly through igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic forms as conditions change.” The cycle has multiple paths, and rock families can transform repeatedly as conditions vary.

source: The rock cycle is not a one-way ladder; rocks can move through many paths and repeat over geologic time. The corrective says: “The cycle has many paths: any rock type can become any other; metamorphic rock can erode to sediment, or melt to magma and re-crystallize as igneous rock.” This path matches a rock that becomes metamorphic, then melts to magma, then crystallizes as igneous rock.
target: Corrective: “The cycle has many paths: any rock type can become any other; metamorphic rock can erode to sediment, or melt to magma and re-crystallize as igneous rock.” Melting to magma is the key bridge back to igneous formation.

source: This is sedimentary rock, not a cooled melt. The corrective says: “Sedimentary rock does not cool from a melt; it forms when loose sediment is deposited, compacted, and cemented (lithified) at low temperatures near the surface.”
target: The corrective is explicit: “Sedimentary rock does not cool from a melt; it forms when loose sediment is deposited, compacted, and cemented (lithified) at low temperatures near the surface.” Sedimentary features record depositional environment; they are not produced by cooling magma.

source: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the classic divergent example. At divergent boundaries, plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created.
target: Worked example trio (from the reading): The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is divergent (sea floor spreading); the Andes are convergent (subduction); the San Andreas Fault is transform. For each, connect the boundary type to what plates do: divergent move away and create new lithosphere; convergent move toward and destroy lithosphere; transform plates slide horizontally past each other.

source: At divergent boundaries, plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created. Plates move over the solid but ductile asthenosphere, not a liquid magma layer.
target: Directly confront the misconception: “Plates move over the solid but ductile asthenosphere, which flows slowly by convection; there is no liquid magma layer carrying them.”

source: Use streak: "Streak examines the color of a powdered mineral." In the hematite example, hematite can look silvery or red, but its streak is always reddish-brown—"the powder color gives it away when the specimen color does not."
target: Worked example walkthrough (minerals): Hematite case—students often misread the specimen’s surface color.
