source: `Dog` is the class name, not one specific dog. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it, for example `d = Dog()`. Per-object data belongs on each instance, not on the class itself.
target: Remember: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.” The option that does d = Dog() then sets d.name matches that rule.

source: Corrective: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.” Storing per-object data on Dog itself is the confusion.
target: This directly confronts the misconception: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.” So class-level data is not the same as per-object attributes on instances.

source: Kernel fact: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.” So methods are shared; attributes are per-instance.
target: The key idea is: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.” So method code is shared, but each instance’s attribute values are separate.

source: The check happens at the top of each pass, not in the middle of the body. So the loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration, and the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.
target: Correct: after each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue. The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.

source: Recursion never terminates when there is no base case that stops the self-calls, and it can also fail when the recursive call does not shrink the input toward the base case.
target: Correct: every recursion needs a base case so the chain of self-calls eventually stops, and each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (for example, `n - 1`). Without that, recursion never terminates and can raise a RecursionError.

source: Reteach one common sticking point: “I can run x = x + 1 like math equality.” Re-rail it as an instruction: In Python = is assignment, not equality; the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one. Then connect to the worked example again: that’s exactly why score becomes 15.
target: In Python, = is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left. So x = x + 1 simply increases x by one, and here score becomes 15.

source: Python uses == to compare values. A single = is assignment, not a test for equality, so the correct form is if score == 100:.
target: The misconception is writing if score = 100: and expecting it to compare. In Python, comparison uses == (two equals signs); a single = is assignment. A condition that asks whether two values are equal must be written score == 100.

source: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; for a counter loop, that means updating n (e.g., n = n - 1 or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.
target: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. The loop test is checked at the top of each iteration, so the update has to happen in the body.

source: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Here, total exists only inside make_total(), so print(total) fails outside the function.
target: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. So you need total = make_total(5).

source: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. So changing one dog's name does not change the other dog's name; only the methods are shared.
target: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it, and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. So each instance has its own attributes, and changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name.

source: Use explicit conversion: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text. The worked example states: “‘Age: ' + str(19) builds 'Age: 19', while 'Age: ' + 19 raises a TypeError because a str and an int cannot be added.”
target: The worked example shows it: 'Age: ' + str(19) builds 'Age: 19'. The incorrect one is 'Age: ' + 19 because a str and an int cannot be added—so convert the number with str() before joining it to text.

source: `int()` removes any fractional part, so `int(3.9)` is `3`. That is the behavior described by the quote: “int() converts a data type to an integer. Any fractional part is removed.”
target: int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3.

source: Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; then 'Age: ' + str(19) produces 'Age: 19'.
target: Python will not silently convert an int into a string inside a + with a str. Convert the number with str() before joining it to text (as in 'Age: ' + str(19)).

source: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; 'Age: ' + str(19) works and produces 'Age: 19'. Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str.
target: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. So `'Age: ' + 19` fails.

source: A while loop repeats based on a condition that is re-checked each time. That matches the reading: 'A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.'
target: Introduce the while loop as: a loop expression (condition) and a loop body. Emphasize “runs … while a given condition … is true” and that the condition is re-checked before each iteration. Use the mental model: check → run body → check again → keep going only if still true.

source: The loop does not interrupt the body halfway through. The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.
target: Correcting the claim: “The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.” So changes inside the body won’t interrupt the already-running iteration.

source: Work example: for i in range(3): print(i). Anchor to: “The range() function produces a sequence of integers”. Trace the output: it prints 0, 1, 2 — three lines, starting at 0 and stopping before 3. Explicitly connect that to “range(n) yields 0 through n-1.”
target: Worked example anchor: “for i in range(3): print(i) prints 0, 1, 2 — three lines, starting at 0 and stopping before 3.” Walk through what range(3) produces, then trace how the loop retrieves objects one at a time. Contrast with the misconception that range(5) means 1 through 5.

source: Functions as reusable code: start from the idea “A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called”. Build the syntax skeleton: def + name + parentheses + colon + indented body. Emphasize that the body does not run at definition time.
target: Functions as reusable code blocks + the two “when does it run?” moments. Introduce def syntax, named/reusable idea, and the call trigger. Anchor quote: “A function is defined using the def keyword”. Emphasize that the body does NOT run at definition time.

source: Scope fundamentals: define scope as “the part of a program where the variable can be accessed.” Contrast local vs global with the anchor quotes: local variables exist only within the function call; global variables are accessible anywhere.
target: Scope map: variable scope is where it can be accessed. Define local vs global with the anchor quotes: “A variable's scope is the part of the program where the variable can be accessed”, “A variable created within a function has local scope and only exists within the function”, and “A variable created outside of a function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program”.

source: The variable was created inside the function call, so it does not exist outside that call. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.
target: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Here, x is created inside make(), so print(x) fails because x is not in global scope.

source: The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. Reassigning x changes x, not the underlying list it came from, so nums stays [10, 20, 30]. To change list contents, index into the list directly.
target: The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, index into the list directly. In this loop, x is reassigned, but nums never gets modified.

source: Defining with def only stores the function; calling square(5) runs the body and returns n * n. Since 5 * 5 = 25, x becomes 25. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.
target: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. The worked example is: def square(n): return n * n ; square(5) runs the body and returns 25.

source: Lists basics: introduce what a list is (ordered collection in square brackets) and how indexing works. Emphasize: indexes begin at 0 and go to one less than the length. Show how to write a list and access individual elements with an index using the anchor quotes: “A list is defined by using square brackets [] with comma separated values within the square brackets” and “Individual list elements can be accessed directly using an index”.
target: Quick re-teach for anyone who arrived cold: what a list is (square brackets with comma-separated values), what an index is, and the key rule “Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.” Anchor quote: “A list is defined by using square brackets [] with comma separated values within the square brackets.”

source: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence, so the last index is 4. `5, because the list has 5 items` is the classic off-by-one mistake.
target: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence. A 5-item list has indices 0..4, so nums[4] is the last element: 50.

source: “Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.” Since inside is local to square(5), print(inside) causes a NameError.
target: Variables created inside a function have local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. So print(y) will fail with a NameError.

source: The correction is that `str` is immutable. To change characters, use a new value: convert to a list of characters for mutation (chars=list(s)), then convert back to a string (s=''.join(chars)), or build a new string using slicing.
target: Immutability focus: address the “try to assign to `s[i]`” idea. Contrast what happens with assignment vs creating a new value. Show mutation-by-conversion at a high level: convert to a list of characters (`chars=list(s)`), mutate `chars`, then convert back to a string with `s=''.join(chars)` (or use slicing to build a new string).

source: The correction is that `str` is immutable. To change characters, use a new value: convert to a list of characters for mutation (chars=list(s)), then convert back to a string (s=''.join(chars)), or build a new string using slicing.
target: This directly targets the misconception: Students try to modify a specific character in a string using assignment (e.g., `s[0] = 'X'`). Instructor explains that `str` is immutable and shows converting to a list of characters for mutation (`chars=list(s)`), then converting back to a string (`s=''.join(chars)`), or using string slicing to build a new string.

source: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length, so a 3-item list’s last index is 2. names[2] returns 'Cy', while names[5] is out of range. The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.
target: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence. For this 3-item list, index 0 is the first item, index 1 is the second, and index 2 is the last. So `names[2]` is `'Cy'`.

source: Python string indexing is 0-based, so s[0] is the first character and s[1] is the second character.
target: String indexing is zero-based, so for a string `s`, `s[0]` is the first character and `s[len(s)-1]` is the last character. That matches the correct last-index formula for length minus 1.

source: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second. The student’s “index 1 is the first element” belief is off by one.
target: This confronts the misconception: Students count the first element as position 1 instead of index 0. The first element is at index 0, so `lst[0]` is the first item and `lst[1]` is the second.

source: Dictionaries vs lists: keys are labels, not positions. Start from the anchor: “A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs.” Explain the key: value syntax {key: value}, and that lookup uses the key rather than numeric index. Contrast with a list where elements are accessed by numeric index.
target: Cold-start recap: what a dictionary is (key → value), why keys matter, and how lookups work. Quick contrast: list uses numeric position; dictionary uses a key. Emphasize: “A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs.”

source: A dictionary is not read by numeric position. It is accessed by key, so `grades['Ava']` returns the value stored under the key `'Ava'`. The corrective is: “Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].”
target: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position. Here the key is 'Ben', so grades['Ben'] returns the value stored under that key (88).

source: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not by position: use d['name'] to retrieve the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0]. Keys are unique, so looking up a key directly selects the single associated value.
target: Your keys are 'name' and 'value', so the correct lookup is by key. The corrective idea is: “Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].”

source: Confronting the misconception: “Students assign two values to the same key and expect both to be kept.” Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry. So grades['Ava'] becomes 97.
target: Keys are unique in a dictionary. Assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry—so grades['Ava'] becomes 97.

source: File I/O walkthrough: cover open() returning a file object; compare read() (reads entire file into a single string), readline() (next single line), and readlines() (list of every line). Emphasize that reading progress matters (so repeated reads behave differently) and that closing matters (or use with). Use the anchor quote: “Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function” from the reading.
target: Core pipeline for file I/O: open a file to get a file object, read or write its contents, then close it. Emphasize that open() returns a file object; read() returns the entire file as a single string; readline() returns the next line; readlines() returns a list of all lines in order. Anchor on: “Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function”.

source: Worked Example (from the reading): with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() . Walk through it exactly: open('data.txt') creates the file object, f.read() reads all of it into text as one string, and the with block closes the file automatically.
target: Worked example and focus points: with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read(). Ground the steps in the provided example and quote it: “The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string”. Then connect to the file object lifecycle: the with block closes automatically even if something goes wrong. Contrast quickly with using open() without with: remember to close at the end.

source: In Python 3, “the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.” So 7 // 2 is the whole-number quotient you want.
target: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5. If you want a whole-number quotient, use `//` for floor division.

source: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; for a counter loop, that means updating n (e.g., n = n - 1 or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.
target: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.

source: Kickoff: what recursion is and when to use it. Anchor on the idea that recursion “uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem,” and that a recursive function “calls itself on a smaller input.” Emphasize the two must-haves: base case + shrinking toward it. Quick mental model: each call is one step closer to a known answer.
target: Recursion foundations: define recursion as reducing a problem to a simpler version of the same problem; introduce base case and termination. Work through the anchor ideas: "Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem" and "A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input". Use factorial as the running example to highlight base case vs recursive step.

source: Reteach (worked example walks through the reading core concept): with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() opens the file, reads all of it into text, and closes it automatically. We re-check the core reading idea: read() reads the entire file into one string, and the file’s reading position advances; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset. Also reinforce: using with ensures the file is closed automatically even if an error occurs.
target: Reteach for students who arrived cold—file reading core concept: use the reading that "with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read()" reads the entire file into a string and closes automatically. Then reteach the “single pass” behavior of read(): after read() hits the end, the next read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset. Connect this to the idea of state/position marker, not randomness. Anchor quote: "The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string".

source: The problem is that the call is not shrinking the input, so the recursion never reaches a stopping point. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.
target: The termination rule is about shrinking toward the base case: "Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached." If the step size skips past your base case inputs, you must adjust the base case and/or the decrement so it’s actually reached.

source: A class is the blueprint for creating objects. Individual objects created from a class are called instances, and each instance carries its own copy of the attributes while the methods are shared by every instance.
target: Quick re-teach (cold start friendly): What is a class vs an object? Anchor quotes: “A class is a blueprint for creating objects” and “Individual objects created of the class type are called instances.” Use a tiny example: class Dog: ...; then a = Dog() and b = Dog(). Emphasize: instances carry their own attribute data; methods are shared.

source: `a = Dog()` and `b = Dog()` create two instances from the class blueprint. The worked example says each instance has its own `name` attribute. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.
target: Worked example: Dog class + two instances. Start from the given anchor idea: “class Dog: defines the blueprint; a = Dog() and b = Dog() are two instances, each with its own name attribute.” Show: set a.name = 'Rex' and b.name = 'Milo' and explain why one change does not change the other (attributes per instance; methods shared). Tie to misconception fixes for storing data on the class and sharing attribute values across instances.

source: Corrective: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.” Storing per-object data on Dog itself is the confusion.
target: Corrective: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.”

source: `n == 0` is the base case: the simplest input solved directly without another call. Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.
target: “Every recursion needs a base case… so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.” Here, n=0 is the simplest input solved directly.

source: Kernel fact: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.” So methods are shared; attributes are per-instance.
target: Kernel correction: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.”

source: `d = Dog()` is the instance creation step. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it, and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. `class Dog:` only defines the blueprint.
target: A class is the blueprint for making objects. You create instances from it, like `d = Dog()`, and per-object data belongs on each instance, not on the class itself.

source: and returns True only if both conditions are true. If either one is false, the whole condition is false.
target: and returns True only if both conditions are true. or needs just one true condition, not flips one condition, and = is assignment.

source: The condition is checked at the top of each iteration, not in the middle of the body. The rest of the current pass still runs before the next check.
target: The condition is checked at the top of each iteration. Even if `count` changes in the middle of the body, the rest of that pass still runs before the next condition check.

source: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Writing def greet(): does not execute the body immediately.
target: Defining a function only stores it. The body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). That corrects the common mistake that def itself executes the body.

source: A for loop visits each element in order. Direct indexing gives one item, not the whole list.
target: Close by connecting access and iteration: direct indexing gets one element, while a for loop walks through the whole list in order.

source: Indexes begin at 0, and the last valid index is one less than the length. That is why a 5-item list uses indexes 0 through 4.
target: Indexes run from 0 to one less than the length. For 5 items, the valid indexes are 0 through 4, so 4 is the last one.

source: A list is written with square brackets [] holding comma-separated values. The other forms are a tuple, a set, or just a comma-separated expression.
target: A list is written with square brackets holding comma-separated values. Parentheses and braces are different forms.

source: Use s[0:3]. The slice starts at index 0 and stops before index 3, so it returns the characters at indices 0, 1, and 2. That is exactly three characters, not four.
target: Work through a few string examples on the board. Show how s[0:3] gives the first three characters, not four, because the slice stops before index 3. Then build a new string from parts instead of trying to change one character in place.

source: readlines() returns a list with every line of the file. readline() gives only the next single line, and read() returns the whole file as one string.
target: If you’re coming in cold, focus on the direction of the data. read() gives the entire file as one string. readline() gives the next single line. readlines() gives a list containing every line. The file keeps a position marker, so repeated reads keep moving forward through the file.

source: Always close the file when done, or use a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs.
target: Always close the file when you are done. A with block does that for you automatically, even if an error occurs.

source: `=` is assignment, not equality. Python evaluates the right side first, then binds the result to the name on the left, so `x` becomes 5.
target: Assignment is not equality. Python evaluates the right side first, then binds the result to the name on the left, so this statement increases x by one.

source: Each comparison needs its own operands, so age > 13 and age < 19 is the valid form. The bare “< 19” option is the documented mistake of skipping the left operand on the second comparison.
target: Each comparison needs its own operands. The corrected form is age > 13 and age < 19. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left.

source: range(5) starts at 0 and stops before 5, so it yields exactly five values: 0 through 4.
target: range(n) starts at 0 and stops before n. So range(5) gives exactly five values: 0 through 4.

source: Calling read() advances the file’s position marker through the file. Once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns an empty string until you reopen the file or reset the position.
target: File reading advances a position marker. Once read() reaches the end, another read() returns an empty string until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

source: Recursion is problem reduction: the function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.
target: For students who came in cold, restate recursion in plain terms: a function solves a task by calling itself on a smaller version of the same task. Then re-check the two common mistakes here: no base case at all, or a recursive call that does not get smaller. Both keep the function from reaching the stop condition.

source: A heuristic is a general framework that helps when time or information is limited. That is different from an exact step-by-step algorithm.
target: Compare solution approaches for a problem. An algorithm is a step-by-step formula that aims for a specific result. A heuristic is a general framework you use when the situation is messy, time is short, or there is too much information to process carefully. Heuristics are not sloppy; they are chosen because they fit the limits of the problem.

source: Calling read() advances the file’s position marker through the file. Once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns an empty string until you reopen the file or reset the position.
target: Reading moves through the file. After read() reaches the end, another read() returns an empty string until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

source: The check happens at the top of each pass, not in the middle of the body. So the loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration, and the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.
target: The loop expression is tested at the top of each iteration. Changing a variable inside the body does not interrupt the current pass; the rest of that pass still runs before the next check.

source: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. Here, n never changes, so the condition stays true and the loop runs forever.
target: A while loop only stops when its condition turns false, so the body has to change something the condition depends on. If the counter never changes, the loop can run forever.

source: Scope depends on where the variable is created. A variable made inside a function is local to that function call, while one made outside any function is global and can be accessed anywhere in the program.
target: For students who arrived cold, restate the core idea without extra machinery. A function is code you name so you can use it again. def sets it up; the body waits until the function is called. Scope tells you where a variable is visible. Local variables belong to the function call that made them. Global variables were created outside functions and can be used across the program. If a local result needs to live on outside the function, return it and save it in a name outside.

source: A local variable exists only during the call that created it. To use the result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.
target: A local variable stays inside the call that created it. To use the result later, the function has to return it and the caller has to capture that returned value.

source:
A classmate says the first item in a list is at position 1. What does Python use for the first element?
lst[1] is the first item
lst[0] is the first item
lst[2] is the first item
lst[1] and lst[0] are both the first item
The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second. Python uses zero-based indexing for lists, not position 1 for the first item.
target: Lists hold an ordered set of values in square brackets. Each element has a position called an index, and Python starts counting at 0. That means the first item is at index 0, the second is at index 1, and the last index is one less than the list’s length.

source: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. Use / when you want a true division result, not an integer result.
target: Switch to types. Every value has a type, and Python can promote types automatically inside a mixed expression. True division with / always returns a float. Floor division with // keeps the whole-number quotient. int() drops the fractional part when converting to an integer.

source: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5. If you want the whole-number quotient, use //, which gives 3.
target: The / operator always returns a float in Python 3, even when both operands look like whole numbers. So 7 / 2 is 3.5. Use // when you want the whole-number quotient.

source: The end index of a slice is exclusive. So s[0:3] returns characters at indices 0, 1, and 2, stopping before index 3.
target: If you arrived cold, rebuild the basics first. A slice s[a:b] gives characters from index a up to but not including b. That end index is exclusive. The same idea shows up any time you pull a piece out of text: you select a range, not a single character, and the original string stays unchanged unless you assign a new value to the variable.

source: In Python 3, / does true division, so it always returns a float. So 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.
target: True division with / always returns a float. For 7 / 2, that is 3.5. The whole-number result comes from //, not /.

source: Indexes begin at 0, and the last valid index is one less than the length. That is why a 5-item list uses indexes 0 through 4.
target: List indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the list. In a 5-item list, the last index is 4, so items[4] is the last element.

source: In Python, = assigns a new value. The right side is computed first, so x + 1 becomes 5, and that value is bound to x.

source: Every recursion needs a base case—a simplest input solved directly without another call—so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. source: A class is the blueprint for creating objects. Individual objects created from a class are called instances, and each instance carries its own copy of the attributes while the methods are shared by every instance.

source: The class is the blueprint, and the pet you build from it is the instance. Attributes belong to each instance, while the class supplies shared methods. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.

source: If you remove the base case, recursion has no stop point. The core corrective is: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.” Without it, the self-calls never end and can overflow the call stack.

source: Start with the core idea of a while loop: it keeps running “while” a loop expression is true, and it re-checks that expression before each new iteration. source: A while loop terminates only if something the condition depends on changes during the loop. source: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. So if `x` becomes 0 in the middle of the body, the remaining statements in that pass still execute before the next check.

source:
Which loop will print `3 2 1` and then stop?
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n + 1
n = 3
while n < 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
n = 3
