source: A class is the blueprint for creating objects, and `a` and `b` are the objects built from it. The mistaken idea is to treat the class itself as an object that stores per-instance data. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.
target: A class is the blueprint for creating objects, and `a` and `b` are individual instances built from that class. The class itself is not the stored data; each instance is. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.

source: For objects, each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name. The class provides the shared methods, but the per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class itself.
target: Each instance carries its own attributes, so one dog's `name` does not overwrite the other's. The shared part is the methods defined by the class, not the per-object data. Clarify that correct behavior depends on control flow and data passed via function calls/returns and side effects, not on local variable names. Use consistent function signatures, check imports and returned values, and ensure modules agree on data formats (types/structures).

source: Start with the definition: a system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables, and a solution assigns values to all variables so every equation holds at the same time. Classify systems by the number of solutions: exactly zero, exactly one, or infinitely many—never exactly two. Translate a couple of quick examples into “what it means geometrically” (meeting lines vs parallel lines) to make consistency/inconsistency feel concrete.
target: Systems as “simultaneous truth.” Define: a system of linear equations is a collection in the same variables; a solution assigns values so that every equation holds at the same time. Classify outcomes: exactly zero, exactly one, or infinitely many solutions (never exactly two). Quick visual analogy: two equations can describe parallel lines (no intersection) or intersect in one point. Connect this to the later goal: decide which case a given system falls into.

source: Over the real numbers, if a linear system has two distinct solutions, then it has infinitely many, because every point on the line through those two solutions also satisfies the system. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet. Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method.
target: Both equations have the same left-hand side but different constants, so the lines are parallel and never meet. That makes the system inconsistent, so it has no solution; the “every system of equations has a solution” belief fails here. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method.

source: Elementary row operations are reversible, so they preserve the solution set. That is why elimination works; the belief that row operations change the solutions is exactly the trap here. Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.
target: Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set, so the transformed matrix represents the same solutions. The mistaken idea that row operations change the solutions is false; elimination works precisely because it does not change the solution set. Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.

source: Pivot positions come from echelon structure during elimination. The size of the entries does not decide pivots, so “the columns with the largest numbers” is the wrong rule.
target: Pivot positions come from echelon structure during elimination: they are the first nonzero entries of the rows. The size of the entries does not decide pivots, so the “largest numbers become pivot columns” belief is wrong.

source:
Consider the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. What is the correct classification?
Consistent, because every system of equations has a solution.
Inconsistent, because the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.
Consistent, because if a system has more than one solution it has some finite number of them.
Inconsistent, because row operations change the solutions of the system.
Over the real numbers, if a linear system has two distinct solutions, then it has infinitely many, because every point on the line through those two solutions also satisfies the system. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet. Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method.
target: Consistency means at least one solution exists; inconsistency means none exist. A linear system can have zero, one, or infinitely many solutions, so the other statements contradict the basic classification. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method.

source: Each elementary row operation is reversible, so it preserves the solution set; that is why elimination works. Pivot columns come from echelon structure, not from the size of the entries, so the “largest numbers” idea is wrong.
target: Pivot columns are determined by echelon structure, not by how large the entries look. You cannot choose them from the biggest numbers, and having two solutions is not a linear-system possibility over the reals. Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.

source: Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms counts as a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included. Geometry is one model, not the definition, so arrows are only one example of vectors. A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.
target: Polynomials satisfy the vector-space axioms under the usual operations, so they are vectors too. The “arrows in 2D or 3D” idea is too narrow, and a subset or line fails unless it contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.

source: The two equations contradict each other, so no assignment can satisfy both at once. This is the classic inconsistent case: “the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.” Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.
target: The two equations are inconsistent: they describe parallel lines that never meet, so no assignment can satisfy both at once. The “every system has a solution” belief breaks here, and the system cannot have exactly two solutions. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.

source: Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. So a finite count larger than one does not happen for linear systems.
target: Once a linear system has two distinct real solutions, every point on the line through them also solves the system, so there are infinitely many. The finite-number belief misses that linear solution sets are whole lines, not just a few isolated points.

source: A linear system cannot stop at two solutions. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.
target: Over the real numbers, two distinct solutions force infinitely many solutions along the whole line through them. A linear system never stops at exactly two solutions, and inconsistency means no solution at all.

source: Start from the definition: an n-by-n matrix A is invertible if there exists a matrix B such that AB = BA = I. Emphasize uniqueness of the inverse (so we write A⁻¹) and the practical meaning: if A is invertible, then for every b the system Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b.
target: Set the goal: invertibility. Start with the definition: an n-by-n matrix A is invertible when there is a matrix B so that AB = BA = I; then B is the unique inverse A⁻¹. Emphasize the “square only” rule and the “exactly when A has n pivots (equivalently, nonzero determinant)” criterion. Connect to systems: if A is invertible, then Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b for every b.

source: To undo AB, you must reverse the order of the two operations, so the inverse is B⁻¹A⁻¹. The belief that (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹ keeps the original order, but undoing two composed operations requires reversing their order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.
target: Worked example (conceptual, no numbers): Start with the idea of undoing a matrix operation. Let A and B be square and assume both inverses exist. We want to 'undo' AB acting on a vector: (AB)x = b. The correct undoing uses order reversal: x = (AB)⁻¹b. Then compute (AB)⁻¹ via the rule (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ (because you must reverse the order of two composed operations). Finish by checking: AB(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A( I )A⁻¹ = I and similarly on the other side.

source: Cover the two “algebra rules” students must not mix up. (1) Inverse of a product reverses order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ (when both inverses exist). (2) Matrix multiplication is not entrywise: the (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Wrap up with the noncommutativity point: AB generally differs from BA; it can equal only in special cases (like identity or powers of the same matrix).
target: Matrix multiplication mechanics that students need for inverses: AB is defined when columns of A match rows of B, and the (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Stress the common traps: (a) multiplication is not entrywise (unlike addition/scalar multiplication) and (b) order matters in products: AB = BA only in special cases (e.g., when one factor is the identity or when both are powers of the same matrix). Tie back to why the inverse of a product reverses order.

source: Determinant properties we’ll use in computation. (1) Multiplicativity: det(AB)=det(A)det(B). (2) Row operations: swapping rows flips sign; scaling a row scales the determinant; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged. Emphasize what is predictable vs what is not (especially additivity).
target: Determinant properties and row operations: Focus on the only property we will lean on for now: det(AB)=det(A)det(B). Then translate the row-operation rules into determinant effects you can use reliably: swapping rows flips sign; scaling a row scales det by the same factor; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged. Demonstrate the logic of each change (sign flip from reversing orientation; scaling multiplies volume; row-addition doesn’t change linear dependence).

source: The determinant tracks invertibility and volume scaling, so small entries do not force a small determinant. The mistaken belief that a matrix with small entries has a small determinant, and a large determinant means a 'big' matrix, confuses entry size with what the determinant actually measures; a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero.
target: Determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling; if it is 0, the matrix is not invertible. Entry size does not determine the determinant: a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero, so the belief that small entries force a small determinant is wrong.

source: No. The (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, which is different from an entrywise product.
target: The (i, j) entry of AB comes from the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. It is not entrywise, and order matters because AB and BA can differ or one may not be defined.

source: Warm-up on what a vector space really is: a set + operations that satisfy the axioms (closure, associativity, commutativity, identity, inverses, distributivity). Emphasize: geometry is not the definition—polynomials, matrices, and functions can be vectors (under the usual operations).
target: Start with the definition: a vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the axioms (closure, associativity, commutativity, identity, inverse, distributivity). Emphasize the two “musts”: it contains a zero vector, and every vector has an additive inverse. We use R^n as the standard example, but we also point out the key idea: geometry is not the definition—vector spaces can be polynomials, matrices, or functions.

source: Subspaces: build the checklist. A subspace is a subset that contains the zero vector AND is closed under addition AND scalar multiplication. Then connect the idea of span: linear combinations of given vectors always form a subspace, and the span is the smallest subspace containing them.
target: Subspaces: A subspace is a subset of a vector space that contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. We connect this to span: the span of a set of vectors (all linear combinations) is always a subspace, and it’s the smallest subspace containing those vectors. We also distinguish “span” from “geometric shape”: a span can be a line, a plane, or a point depending on independence (e.g., two parallel vectors collapse). Finally, we preview closure failures: a line not through the origin misses the zero vector and cannot be a subspace.

source: A plane through the origin is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so it is a subspace. The tempting plane x+y+z=1 fails because it misses the zero vector and is not closed under scaling; not every line or plane in R^3 is a subspace.
target: The plane z = 0 passes through the origin, so it contains the zero vector and stays closed under addition and scalar multiplication. The other geometric choices miss the origin; only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces, and others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling. The positive-x set is not a subspace either, because a subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

source: Since w = 2v, the two vectors are parallel, so their span collapses to a line. The tempting “always a plane” belief fails when the vectors are dependent; the span’s dimension depends on independence.
target: Since v and w are independent, their linear combinations form a plane through the origin. The tempting claim that the span of two vectors is always a plane fails when the vectors are parallel or one is zero; then the span collapses to a line or a point, so the span's dimension depends on independence. The other choices miss this dependence on linear independence. Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition. Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.

source:
Suppose a linear system over the real numbers has two distinct solutions. What must be true?
It has exactly two solutions.
It has infinitely many solutions.
It has no solution because two solutions is impossible.
It has only one solution after row reduction.
A linear system cannot stop at two solutions. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.
target: Over the real numbers, two distinct solutions force infinitely many solutions: the whole line through them solves the system. The finite-number belief is wrong for linear systems; once there are two distinct solutions, there are infinitely many.

source: Start with the definition: what it means for a set of vectors to be linearly independent (only the trivial combination gives the zero vector). Emphasize the contrast: a nontrivial combination equal to zero is a dependence relation. Quick mental check: what happens if the set contains the zero vector? (It’s automatically dependent.)
target: Kickoff: independence vs dependence. Start with the definition: a set is linearly independent only if the only way to make the zero vector is using all zero coefficients; otherwise you have a dependence relation. Quick check: why a set containing the zero vector is automatically dependent. Tie to span/subspace as needed: dependence means some vector is redundant because it can be written as a combination of the others.

source:
Which statement must be true for any set of 4 vectors in R^3?
The set is independent because the vectors are different from each other.
The set is independent because more vectors give more independence.
The set is dependent because any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent.
The set is a basis because every spanning set of 4 vectors in R^3 is automatically independent.
In R^3, any set with more than 3 vectors is automatically dependent. Adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it, so the first two choices miss the dimension limit. Distinct vectors can still be dependent — (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) are pairwise different yet dependent; independence is about redundancy, not distinctness.
target: Any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent, so four vectors in R^3 cannot be independent. Distinctness does not help here, and adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it. Distinct vectors can still be dependent — (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) are pairwise different yet dependent; independence is about redundancy, not distinctness. Spaces have infinitely many bases — R^2 is spanned by the standard basis but equally by (1, 1) and (1, -1); only the SIZE of a basis is fixed.

source: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero, and -7 is nonzero. The sign does not block invertibility; only a zero determinant does. The determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size, so a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero.
target: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero, and -3 is nonzero. The sign does not block invertibility; only a zero determinant does.

source: Rank counts pivots after row reduction, and this reduced matrix has two pivot columns. The “nonzero rows in the original matrix” idea is wrong because a matrix full of nonzero entries can still have rank 1 if its rows are proportional. Rank never exceeds the smaller of the row and column counts, and dependence among columns lowers it further.
target: Reteach core concept by re-walking the same conceptual worked example (the definition-based walkthrough): Col(A)=span(columns of A)=all b such that Ax=b is consistent, and Nul(A)=all x such that Ax=0. Then we re-assert what rank means: rank(A)=dimension(Col(A))=number of pivot columns after row reduction, and nullity(A)=dimension(Nul(A)). Finally we use the corrective: ‘Rank counts pivots AFTER row reduction; a matrix full of nonzero entries can still have rank 1 if its rows are proportional.’

source: Start with the meaning of a system: a collection of linear equations in the same variables, and a solution means you assign values to every variable so that every equation holds simultaneously. Then classify systems: a linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two. Define consistent (at least one solution) vs inconsistent (no solutions). Finish by stating the workflow we will use: represent the system as an augmented matrix and solve by row reduction.
target: Warm start: recall what “linear system” means and how solution counts work. Stress: a linear system is consistent if it has at least one solution and inconsistent if it has none; it has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two. Then connect to matrices: every linear system can be represented as an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction.

source: Worked example (row reduction to classify solutions): Take the augmented system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. When you row-reduce the augmented matrix, you end up with a contradiction row like 0x + 0y = 1 (equivalently 0=nonzero), so the system is inconsistent and has zero solutions. This is exactly the distinction behind the statement: “A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.”
target: Worked example (reading core: solution counts via row reduction, plus consistency): Consider the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. Write both equations as two rows in an augmented matrix and row-reduce. You will get a contradiction row (same left-hand side, different constant), meaning there are no solutions. Conclude: it is inconsistent. Emphasize the misconception repair: "A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet."

source:
A student writes the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. What should you conclude?
It is consistent, because every system of equations has a solution.
It is inconsistent, because the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.
It has exactly two solutions, because the equations agree on a pair of points.
It has infinitely many solutions, because two equations in two variables usually do.
The two equations contradict each other, so no assignment can satisfy both at once. This is the classic inconsistent case: “the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.” Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.
target: The two equations have the same left-hand side but different constants, so they represent parallel lines with no intersection. That makes the system inconsistent. The mistaken belief that every system of equations has a solution is false here: x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent because the equations describe parallel lines that never meet. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.

source:
A linear system in real variables has two distinct solutions. What must be true?
It has some finite number of solutions, because more than one solution can still stop after two.
It has no solution, because two answers mean the equations contradict each other.
It has infinitely many solutions, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.
It has exactly one solution, because row reduction can collapse extra solutions into a single answer.
Over the real numbers, two distinct solutions force infinitely many: the whole line through those two points also solves the linear system. So it cannot be a finite count like 2 or 4. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.
target: Over the real numbers, two distinct solutions force the entire line between them to solve the same linear system, so there are infinitely many solutions. The mistaken belief that more than one solution means some finite number of them is wrong: once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.

source: Reteach using the same worked example (A = [[2,0],[0,3]]): re-walk the steps but stop for misconception repairs. First, explicitly test the wrong idea: ‘Is the zero vector an eigenvector?’ For x=0, Ax=λx is automatically true but eigenvectors are required to be nonzero—so it “holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.” Second, test the wrong idea about zero eigenvalues: explain that λ=0 only tells you there exists some nonzero x with Ax=0 (singular matrix), not that A=0. Finish by restating the workflow: compute λ from det(A−λI)=0, then compute eigenvectors from (A−λI)x=0, always using x≠0.
target: Reteach with the same worked example A = [[2,0],[0,3]] (walking it step-by-step again): Start from Ax = λx and test e1 and e2 to get eigenvalues 2 and 3. Then explicitly address the common wrong turn: “The zero vector is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.” Reteach the correction using the definition: eigenvectors must be nonzero—A·0 = λ·0 is true but “holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.” Finish by stating: because there is no eigenvalue 0 here, the matrix is invertible.

source: A zero eigenvalue means the matrix is not invertible, not that it is the zero matrix. The zero-vector belief fails because eigenvectors must be nonzero, so A0=0 does not count as an eigenvector statement. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix. A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.
target: A zero eigenvalue means there is some nonzero vector x with Ax = 0, so the matrix is singular. It does not force the whole matrix to be zero; one nonzero vector sent to zero is enough. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.

source:
Suppose a 3×3 matrix has three eigenvectors v1, v2, v3 that belong to three distinct eigenvalues. What follows?
They are automatically linearly independent.
They must be the zero vector if the eigenvalues are distinct.
The matrix must be the zero matrix.
The matrix cannot be diagonalizable.
Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent. That fact is stronger than any guess from the entries of the matrix, and it does not require the matrix to be zero. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix. A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.
target: Three linearly independent eigenvectors in a 3×3 matrix meet the exact criterion for diagonalizability. They do not force invertibility or make the matrix the identity; the eigenvalues can still vary. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix. A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.

source: Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent. That fact is stronger than any guess from the entries of the matrix, and it does not require the matrix to be zero. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix. A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.
target: Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent. The zero vector is excluded from eigenspaces, so it cannot be used to make the vectors dependent or to support the zero-matrix claim. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix. A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.

source: A zero eigenvalue means the matrix is not invertible, not that it is the zero matrix. The zero-vector belief fails because eigenvectors must be nonzero, so A0=0 does not count as an eigenvector statement. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix. A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.
target: A zero eigenvalue means there is a nonzero vector x with Ax = 0, so A is not invertible. That does not force every entry to be 0; a matrix can be singular without being zero. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.

source: RETEACH WORKED EXAMPLE: Re-walk the same least-squares geometric example step-by-step, this time focusing on the two common mistakes. First, address “Least squares finds an exact solution”: show that minimizing ||b−Ax|| means Ax̂ generally differs from b, because “being closest is not being equal.” Second, address “Best-fit line must pass through the data points”: explain that least squares minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps, so it can miss every single data point. End by stating the projection view again: Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.
target: Reteach worked example (projection viewpoint): Re-walk the same least-squares story—“Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.” Then explicitly contrast the two common errors: (a) Least squares does *not* find an exact solution to Ax=b in general; it minimizes the residual length, so Ax̂ generally differs from b. (b) The best-fit line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps and can miss every single data point. End by restating: closest-in-column-space is the definition, not equality to b.

source: The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps and can miss every single data point. Best fit is about minimizing total squared error, not forcing the line through the data.
target: The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps, and that line can miss every point in the data set. A best-fit line does not have to pass through the data points; exact interpolation is a different goal. It minimizes the residual; the fitted values Ax̂ generally differ from b — being closest is not being equal.

source: Reteach one worked example from earlier: revisit x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. We’ll explicitly show the key row-reduction step that produces a contradictory row, then state the classification: inconsistent = 0 solutions. Wrap by matching it to the exact corrective idea: 'A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.'
target: Reteach worked example (systems again): Walk through the same row-reduction logic from the earlier worked example—how the final row form determines whether the system is inconsistent, has one solution, or has infinitely many. Repeat the key corrective: “A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.” Then show how row reduction detects that situation through an impossible equation (0 = nonzero).

source: Start with the definition: a system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables, and a solution assigns values to all variables so every equation holds at the same time. Classify systems by the number of solutions: exactly zero, exactly one, or infinitely many—never exactly two. Translate a couple of quick examples into “what it means geometrically” (meeting lines vs parallel lines) to make consistency/inconsistency feel concrete.
target: Set up the big idea: a system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables; a solution assigns a value to each variable so that every equation holds simultaneously. Classify systems as consistent vs inconsistent and emphasize the key fact: a linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two.

source: Move to augmented matrices as the compact representation. Explain that every linear system can be represented as an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction. Introduce echelon form vocabulary: pivot, pivot positions, and free vs basic variables (at the level of reading off solutions). Emphasize the reading: pivot positions determine which variables are constrained and which are free.
target: Walk through a compact representation idea (augmented matrix) and connect it to row reduction: “Every linear system can be represented compactly as an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction.” Then show one small elimination flow to reach echelon form so students can see what 'reading off solutions' means at a high level (no heavy new theory yet).

source: Introduce row reduction at the matrix level. State the allowed elementary row operations: swap two rows, scale a row by a nonzero constant, and add a multiple of one row to another. Emphasize the core invariance: elementary row operations do not change the solution set of the system represented by the matrix. Then define echelon form and pivots: a pivot is the first nonzero entry of a row in echelon form; pivot positions determine which variables are basic and which are free. Close with the uniqueness fact: reduced row echelon form is unique even though different elimination paths can be taken.
target: Teach row reduction mechanics and invariants: define elementary row operations (swap rows, scale a row by a nonzero constant, add a multiple of one row to another). Core correctness: elementary row operations do not change the solution set. Give the pivot idea: a pivot is the first nonzero entry of a row in echelon form; pivot positions determine which variables are basic and which are free.

source: Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector, and that includes polynomials, matrices, and functions. The arrow picture is useful geometry, but it is one model, not the definition. The other options repeat the misconception that vectors are only arrows, or that any subset of R^n is automatically a vector space. A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.
target: Polynomials form a vector space under the usual operations, so they satisfy the axioms. The arrow option is too narrow: “anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included.” A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.

source: A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; this line does not. The belief that any subset of R^n is a vector space fails on those basic axioms; a line not through the origin fails all three.
target: This line does not pass through the origin, so it misses the zero vector and fails closure under addition and scalar multiplication. “Any subset of R^n is a vector space” is the wrong belief; a subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under those operations.

source: Each elementary row operation is reversible, so it preserves the solution set; that is exactly why elimination works. The belief that row operations change the solutions confuses a new matrix with a new system. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.
target: Adding a multiple of one row to another is an elementary row operation, and it preserves the solution set. The wrong belief is that “row operations change the solutions of the system”; elimination works precisely because the solution set stays the same. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.

source: Pivot columns come from pivot positions in echelon form. They are determined by elimination structure, not by entry size.
target: Pivot columns come from pivot positions in echelon form, not from how large the numbers are. The size-based idea is a distraction; “pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination.”

source:
Using A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]], what do you get if you compute BA instead of AB?
[[19, 22], [43, 50]] because AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers
[[23, 34], [31, 46]] because the order matters in matrix products
[[6, 8], [10, 12]] because matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition
BA is not defined because matrix products are never commutative
Here BA is defined, but it is not the same as AB: order matters in matrix products. The commutative-looking option repeats the mistaken “AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers” belief, which only works in special cases. The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation. Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.
target: The (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, which gives [[19, 22], [43, 50]]. The entrywise answers reuse the wrong belief that multiplication works like addition; that is a different operation. The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation. Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix. Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.

source: Pivot positions come from the echelon form: the first nonzero entry in a row is the pivot, not the largest numbers. The idea “largest numbers” confuses arithmetic size with elimination structure. And in matrix products, order matters, so AB = BA only in special cases (e.g., one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix).
target: Pivot positions come from the echelon pattern created during elimination, not from entry size. The “largest numbers” option repeats the wrong belief directly; that is not how pivot columns are determined. Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.

source: Start from the definition: an n-by-n matrix A is invertible if there exists a matrix B such that AB = BA = I. Emphasize uniqueness of the inverse (so we write A⁻¹) and the practical meaning: if A is invertible, then for every b the system Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b.
target: Start with the definition: for an n-by-n matrix A, being invertible means there exists a matrix B such that AB = BA = I. Emphasize uniqueness of the inverse A⁻¹ and that invertibility exists exactly when A has n pivots (equivalently, the determinant is nonzero). Connect invertibility to solving systems: if A is invertible then Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b for every b.

source: Two equal rows force a zero determinant, so the matrix is nonzero yet not invertible. A square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse.
target: Equal rows make the determinant zero, so this square matrix is nonzero yet has no inverse. This catches the belief that every nonzero matrix has an inverse: a square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse.

source: Determinant properties we’ll use in computation. (1) Multiplicativity: det(AB)=det(A)det(B). (2) Row operations: swapping rows flips sign; scaling a row scales the determinant; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged. Emphasize what is predictable vs what is not (especially additivity).
target: Determinant properties via row operations (predictable changes): swapping rows flips sign; scaling a row scales the determinant; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the determinant unchanged. Walk through the logic: these operations correspond to controlled changes in the transformation, so the determinant updates predictably.

source: The determinant tracks invertibility and volume scaling, so small entries do not force a small determinant. The mistaken belief that a matrix with small entries has a small determinant, and a large determinant means a 'big' matrix, confuses entry size with what the determinant actually measures; a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero.
target: The determinant tracks invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size. A matrix of large numbers can still have determinant zero, so small entries do not guarantee a small determinant, and large numbers do not guarantee a big matrix in the determinant sense.

source: Large entries do not prevent determinant 0; the determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size. That is why a matrix of large numbers can still collapse area or volume to zero.
target: The matrix [[50,50],[50,50]] has large entries but dependent rows, so its determinant is zero. That matches the correction: the determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size; a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero.

source: Swapping rows flips the sign of the determinant. The row-operation rule is specific: row addition leaves it unchanged, scaling a row scales it, and swapping rows multiplies it by -1.
target: Adding a multiple of one row to another is a determinant-preserving row operation. Swapping rows flips the sign, and scaling a row scales the determinant, but this specific move leaves it unchanged.

source: Pick a subset S of R^2 and explain which vector-space or subspace test fails: does S contain the zero vector, is it closed under addition, and is it closed under scalar multiplication?
target: Worked example (vector-space vs. not): Let S = {(a,b) ∈ R^2 : a + b = 1}. Test the subspace conditions (using the vector-space axioms idea): does S contain the zero vector? The zero vector (0,0) does not satisfy 0+0=1, so S fails immediately. Also, closure fails: (1,0) and (0,1) are in S, but their sum (1,1) is not in S because 1+1≠1. Conclude: S is not a vector space (and hence not a subspace of R^2).

source: Subspaces + span quick framework: (a) subspace test = contains 0 and is closed under addition + scalar multiplication, (b) span is the smallest subspace containing vectors, (c) watch the two common traps: not every line/plane is a subspace; the span of two vectors isn’t automatically a plane—it depends on whether the vectors are independent (or parallel/zero).
target: Move to subspaces: A subspace is a subset of a vector space that contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Use the span idea: the span of a set of vectors (all linear combinations) is always a subspace; it is the smallest subspace containing those vectors. Connect this to typical geometric “lines/planes” mistakes: ask when a line/plane is guaranteed to be a subspace (only those through the origin satisfy the zero-vector requirement).

source: Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector, and that includes polynomials, matrices, and functions. The arrow picture is useful geometry, but it is one model, not the definition. The other options repeat the misconception that vectors are only arrows, or that any subset of R^n is automatically a vector space. A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.
target: Polynomials fit the vector-space axioms under the usual operations. The other choices miss the key tests: a subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication, and vectors are not restricted to arrows. Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition. Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling. source: Scope fundamentals: define scope as “the part of a program where the variable can be accessed.” Contrast local vs global with the anchor quotes: local variables exist only within the function call; global variables are accessible anywhere.

source: Worked example walkthrough again (functions & scope): start from this helper idea—def square(n): return n * n. Then ask: (1) Does defining it run the body? source: File I/O big idea: open → use the file contents → close. Walk through what open() returns (a file object), and preview the three reads we’ll use: read() (entire file string), readline() (next single line), readlines() (list of all lines). Anchor with: “Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function”.
target: Goal: file input/output. We’ll treat a file as something you must open, use, and close. Anchor: “Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function”. We’ll also note what open() returns (a file object), and what the common reading methods return (read() returns a single string; readline() returns the next line; readlines() returns a list of lines).

source: Worked Example (from the reading): with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() . Walk through it exactly: open('data.txt') creates the file object, f.read() reads all of it into text as one string, and the with block closes the file automatically.
target: Worked example (read the whole file safely): with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read(). Walk through what happens: open() creates a file object; f.read() reads all contents into text; the with block closes the file automatically. Anchor from the reading: “The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string”.

source: `with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read()` reads the whole file into one string and closes it automatically. Always close the file when done, or use a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs.
target: Reteach the same worked example to prevent two common bugs: using read() twice and forgetting to close. We’ll work through: with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read(). Then discuss what would happen if you tried f.read() again on the same open file: the reading cursor is already at the end, so the second read() returns ''. And we’ll reinforce the safety of the with block: “Always close the file when done, or open it in a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs.”

source: readlines() returns a list with every line of the file. readline() gives only the next single line, and read() returns the whole file as one string.
target: `read()` reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string. The list-of-lines result belongs to `readlines()`, while `readline()` gives just one line.

source: Always close the file when done, or open it in a `with` statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs. The `with` block is the safest pattern because it prevents leaving the resource open.
target: The safe pattern is to close the file when you are done, or use `with` so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs. Leaving it open is the exact resource leak this lesson warns about.

source: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not by position, so d['name'] retrieves the value stored under the key 'name' (not d[0]). And since keys are unique, assigning to an existing key overwrites the previous value instead of allowing duplicate keys.
target: Dictionaries can’t keep both values for the same key because keys are unique. Assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value, and you still access dictionary entries by key (like `d['name']`), not by numeric position such as `d[0]`.

source: Kickoff: what recursion is and when to use it. Anchor on the idea that recursion “uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem,” and that a recursive function “calls itself on a smaller input.” Emphasize the two must-haves: base case + shrinking toward it. Quick mental model: each call is one step closer to a known answer.
target: Mini-lecture: Recursion essentials. Anchor quotes: “Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem” and “A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input.” Emphasize the two requirements students must always check: (1) base case exists, (2) every call moves toward it by shrinking the input.

source: The outer code cannot read a local variable directly. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.
target: A function’s local variables only exist during the call that created them, so you can’t use them outside the function unless the function returns a result. In other words, the caller must capture the returned value. This is separate from how read() depends on the file’s position marker. Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

source: A class is the blueprint for creating objects. Individual objects created from a class are called instances, and each instance carries its own copy of the attributes while the methods are shared by every instance.
target: Classes: define what a class is (blueprint for objects) and what an instance is (a specific object created from the class). Anchor the key behavior/data idea: each instance carries its own copy of attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared.

source: Instance attributes are separate per object, so changing one Dog’s name won’t change another Dog’s name. Even though methods are shared from the class, the data each instance carries stays on that instance. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.
target: Each Dog instance has its own attributes, so changing one instance’s name doesn’t change another Dog’s name. Only the methods are shared across instances via the class. The class is the blueprint (e.g. d = Dog()), and the per-object data lives on each instance.

source: Every recursion needs a base case, a simplest input solved directly without another call, so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as `greet()`. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.
target: Recursion must have a base case—a simplest input solved directly—so the self-calls eventually stop. Each recursive call also needs to move toward that base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or it will never be reached. And defining a function with def only stores it; it runs when you call it (like greet()).

source: You’re looking for the blueprint relationship: “A class is a blueprint for creating objects.” Then, “Individual objects created of the class type are called instances.”

source:

Only the methods; each instance has its own copy of the attributes
Only the attributes; each instance has its own copy of methods
Both attributes and methods, since they come from the same class
Nothing is shared; instances are completely independent of class definitions

source: `a = Dog()` and `b = Dog()` create two instances from the class blueprint. The worked example says each instance has its own `name` attribute. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.

source: int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3. It does not round, and it does not turn the number into a string. In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.

source: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false. An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false. That gives you one chosen branch.
target: Conditionals + flow control: if vs else. Explain: an if runs its body only when the condition is True; else runs when the if condition is False. Anchor quote: “If the condition is true, the body is executed. If the condition is false, the body is not executed.” Emphasize exactly one branch in if-else: “When an if-else statement is executed, one and only one of the branches is taken”.

Worked example: if temp > 100: print('boiling') else: print('not boiling') — walk through two cases: when temp is 120, condition is True so the if branch runs; when temp is 90, condition is False so the else branch runs. Then connect to reading of boolean conditions as answers to “true/false questions”.

source: Boolean logic for compound conditions. Define and/or/not exactly in terms of truth values. Emphasize and = True only if both conditions are true; or = True if either is true; not inverts a single condition. Use the anchor quote: “The and operator takes two condition operands and returns True if both conditions are true.”
target: Boolean logic for compound conditions: and, or, not. State what each operator returns: and is True only if both are true; or is True if either is true; not inverts a single condition. Anchor quote: “The and operator takes two condition operands and returns True if both conditions are true.” Show a compound-condition skeleton students can reuse: (cond1) and (cond2), (cond1) or (cond2).

source: We walk through the worked example: def square(n): return n * n. source: Scope triage mini-lab: give 3 short code snippets (one with a local variable read outside; one with a global variable read inside; one that returns a computed value so it can be used outside). Students predict outcomes (value vs NameError) and justify using “variable’s scope is the part of the program where it can be accessed.”
target: Scope prediction mini-lab (quick pairs). Students read short code snippets and predict what they can access and what errors appear. Include cases like: variable created inside a function and then referenced outside; and variable created at top level referenced inside. Students write short answers: “NameError?” and “accessible or not?” Tie back to: “A variable created within a function has local scope and only exists within the function” and “A variable created outside of a function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program”.

source: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly three values. That is why the loop prints 0, 1, 2 in order. The belief that range(3) produces 1 through 3 is wrong because range(3) starts at 0 and stops before 3.

source: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Here, total exists only inside make_total(), so print(total) fails outside the function.
target: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; in A, total is local to make_total(), so print(total) outside would fail. To use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.

source: Lists overview: show lists as ordered collections written with square brackets. Emphasize the key syntax: square brackets [] with comma-separated values, and that each element has an index that begins at 0. Use the anchor quote: “A list is defined by using square brackets [] with comma separated values within the square brackets”. Briefly preview: we’ll do direct indexing, then iteration with a for loop.
target: Lists as ordered collections: introduce list syntax with square brackets and comma-separated values. Emphasize that each element has an index starting at 0, and that you access elements directly using an index. Anchor with: “A list is defined by using square brackets [] with comma separated values within the square brackets” and “Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.”

source: In Python, indexes start at 0 and end at length minus 1, so a 3-item list has valid indexes 0, 1, and 2; lst[3] is out of range.
target: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length, so a 3-item list ends at index 2. `names[3]` is out of range, and the first element is not position 1 in Python lists.

source: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range. The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.
target: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second. That’s why assuming “5 is the last” for a 5-item list is off—indexes run from 0 to length minus 1.

source: A for loop can iterate through a list by visiting each element in order. That is the point of the loop: it handles the whole sequence one item at a time.
target: A `for` loop can iterate through the list itself, visiting each element in order. The other choices treat the list like a number or a single string element instead of a collection of values.

source: Open with a quick contrast: lists are ordered and accessed by numeric index; dictionaries are labeled and accessed by key. Read this aloud: "A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs" and connect it to the mental model “I know the label, so I ask for the value by that label.”
target: Open with the idea of dictionaries as key→value storage (not position). Show the curly-brace syntax and emphasize that lookup happens by key. source: Worked example: grades = {'Ava': 95, 'Ben': 88}; show grades['Ava'] is 95, then show grades['Ava'] = 97 overwrites the old value (the key stays the same). Tie to the idea: lookups use keys, and duplicate keys are not allowed—assigning to an existing key replaces its stored value.

source: The key `'Ava'` maps directly to 95, so that is the value returned. `grades[0]` is the tempting list idea, but dictionaries are accessed by key, not position.
target: `grades['Ava']` looks up the value stored under the key 'Ava', which is 95. The numeric-position idea is a list habit; dictionaries are accessed by key, not position.

target: Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry. That’s why the second assignment replaces Ava’s old score with the new one.

source: `.strip()` removes whitespace from the ends and returns a new string, so the assigned result is `'Python'`. Strings are immutable, so the original text is not modified in place.

source: Launch recursion: define it using the reading’s framing—“Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem”—and connect it to the mechanics: a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input, continuing until it’s small enough to solve directly (base case). Emphasize the termination requirement: without a base case that stops self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.
target: Recursion basics: define recursion as solving a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem, and emphasize the two ingredients: (1) a base case that stops the self-calls, and (2) a recursive step that calls itself on a smaller input. Anchor with the idea that “Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem,” and explicitly connect it to termination: “without it the calls would never stop.”

source: Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem, for example `n - 1`. Always close the file when done, or open it in a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs.

source: Reteach worked example by walking one more time through the reading’s Dog example to confront blueprint-vs-instance confusion. Use the exact pattern: “class Dog: defines the blueprint; a = Dog() and b = Dog() are two instances.” Then explicitly contrast: the class is not the place to store per-dog data; per-object data lives on each instance. Do a quick side-by-side change: set a.name and check that b.name stays the same—methods are shared, but attributes are per instance.

Reteach one worked example (walk it again carefully): Use the exact Dog example again.

Re-state: Dog is the blueprint; a = Dog() and b = Dog() are instances.
Ask: If you set a.name = 'Fido', does b.name change? Why or why not?
Then guide the repair explicitly: “Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.” Close by reinforcing: per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.

source: Instance attributes are separate per object, so changing one Dog’s name won’t change another Dog’s name. Even though methods are shared from the class, the data each instance carries stays on that instance. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.

source: Each instance has its own attributes, so setting `a.name` does not change `b.name`. The shared part is the methods defined by the class, not the attribute values. source: Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. target: Every recursion needs a base case that solves the simplest input directly. Without that stop, the chain of self-calls never ends, so the call stack keeps growing.

source: When a recursive function lacks a base case, the self-calls never stop and the call stack overflows. In classes, each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not affect another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.
target: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. source: A class is the blueprint: you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()). The per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class, because the class defines behavior while instances store their own state. Each instance carries its own attributes, so assigning name on one object doesn’t make another object inherit it. The class mainly supplies shared methods, not shared per-object data.

source: Expressions and types: every value has a type (int, float, str). Expressions combine values, and Python uses implicit type conversion inside mixed expressions. We’ll focus on the two error-makers: (1) / vs // in Python 3 (7 / 2 returns 3.5, not 3), and (2) joining numbers to text requires converting the number to str first (e.g., 'Age: ' + str(19)).
target: Expressions and types: every value has a data type; expressions combine values. Explain conversion: explicit conversion functions like str() and int(), plus implicit type conversion inside mixed expressions. Use the anchor quotes: “explicit type conversion to convert one data type to another” and “The Python interpreter uses implicit type conversion...”. Then cover string building and the need for str() with the worked example: 'Age: ' + str(19) works; 'Age: ' + 19 raises a TypeError.

source: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. This confronts the exact misconception that `/` does integer division because the operands look like whole numbers.
target: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. The important distinction is that `int()` truncates, while `//` performs integer (floor) division.

source: Conditionals mechanics: if runs only when the condition is true; else runs only when the if condition is false. Emphasize the “one and only one branch is taken” idea, and reinforce what a condition actually is (an expression that evaluates to True/False).
target: Re-introduce conditionals as “choose which block to run.” Contrast plain `if` vs `if-else` using the anchor idea: when `if-else` runs, one and only one branch is taken. Emphasize that the condition must evaluate to True/False.

source: Reteach the core concept with one worked example again, as a trace: use the same example if temp > 100: print('boiling') else: print('not boiling'). source: The if-else statement takes one branch or the other. Here, the else branch runs only when temp > 100 is false, so the program prints boiling for true and not boiling for false.
target: The if body runs only when the condition is true; otherwise the else clause runs. Since temp > 100 is false at 95, the program prints 'not boiling'.

source: In Python 3, / does true division, so it always returns a float. So 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.
target: True division always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5. The whole-number result belongs to //, not /.

source: In Python = is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one. That is why the statement changes x instead of comparing two values.
target: In Python = is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one. It does not mean “compare x to x + 1”; it updates x with the computed value.

source: str(19) makes the number text, so the string concatenation works. A bare 19 would raise a TypeError because Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str.

Anchor the wording with: “A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true.”

source: Worked example re-teach (from the reading): “n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1 prints 3, 2, 1 and then stops when n reaches 0.” Walk the trace step-by-step: show each time you evaluate the loop condition, then execute the body, then update n, then re-check the condition again. Anchor with: “At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again.”
target: Work the provided counter example line-by-line: n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1. Show the outputs 3, 2, 1 and emphasize two checks students often miss: (1) the condition is evaluated again before each iteration, and (2) the body updates n so the condition eventually becomes false. Use the anchor quotes: “At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again” and “the loop body must make progress toward ending the condition.”

source: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. So the condition is not re-checked the instant a variable changes in the body.
target: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. That’s why you must update variables inside the body so the condition can eventually become false.

source: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; for a counter loop, that means updating n (e.g., n = n - 1 or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.
target: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. Without that update, the top-of-loop test can keep passing forever.

source: Reteach worked example (for students arriving cold): use the given while-loop example n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1. source: Launch recursion: define it using the reading’s framing—“Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem”—and connect it to the mechanics: a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input, continuing until it’s small enough to solve directly (base case). source: Every recursion needs a base case—a simplest input solved directly without another call—so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. Without it, the recursion never terminates and keeps calling itself indefinitely.
target: Every recursion needs a base case—a simplest input solved directly without another call—so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. If your recursion never reaches that stopping point (for example, it never shrinks toward the base case), it will keep calling itself forever.

source: Every recursion needs a base case, a simplest input solved directly without another call, so the chain of self-calls eventually stops. Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.

source: Functions as reusable code: start from the idea “A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called”. Build the syntax skeleton: def + name + parentheses + colon + indented body. Emphasize that the body does not run at definition time.
target: Functions as reusable code + “when does the body run?” We’ll anchor on the idea: “A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called” and “A function is defined using the def keyword.” Build intuition: define with def (name + parentheses + colon + indented body), then call by name. We’ll also connect scope: “A variable's scope is the part of the program where the variable can be accessed.”

source: A variable created inside a function has local scope. It cannot be accessed outside the function because it belongs to that call.
target: Local vs global scope inside functions. Emphasize: variables created within a function have local scope and only exist within the function; variables created outside have global scope and can be accessed anywhere. Walk through a quick read/print mental model: if you try to use a local variable outside the function, you don’t have a valid variable binding in that scope.

source: Worked example walkthrough: square. Start from the reading-style example: def square(n): return n * n. Call it as square(5) to get 25, then connect it to scope—variables created inside the function are local to that call. Follow-up micro-check: if you try to use the inside variable outside without returning it, you will not have access (local scope).
target: Worked example reteach: the reading’s square function. Start with: def square(n): return n * n. Point out that defining it just stores the function; nothing inside runs yet. Then call square(5) to trigger the body and return 25. Finally, discuss scope with this example: n is local to each call to square; if you try to use n outside, it’s not available unless you return a value and capture it in the caller.

source: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Here, greet() is the step that triggers the code inside the function.
target: Defining a function just stores it; nothing in the function body runs until you call it (for example, `greet()`). If there is no call to `greet()`, you won’t execute its prints—so only `done` appears. Any variables defined inside the function exist only during the call and must be returned to be used outside.

source: Writing a `def` only defines and stores the function; it doesn’t run the function body. The body executes when you call the function by name (for example, `greet()`), not when you write `def greet():`. Also, local variables exist only during the function call, so to use a computed value outside the function you must `return` it and have the caller capture that return value.
target: The function body has local scope: variables like `text` exist only during the specific call that created them. Defining the function itself only stores it; the body runs only when you call it by name (such as `greet()`). To use a computed result outside the function, return it and assign or print the returned value.
